#8791. How to Start a Workout When You Really Don’t Feel Like It (The Bridge Task Method)

If you can’t get yourself to start a workout after a long day, the problem might not be the workout itself. It’s the gear shift from “couch” to “go.”

A bridge task is a small, neutral action (not fun, not hard, just…meh) that you put in between the two so the jump is smaller.

Below is the 5-step version one of our coaching clients uses with her own students, plus a free worksheet to map your own.

A few weeks ago I was talking with Tabitha, a Nerd Fitness coaching client, about a challenge a lot of people face. ​ Some quick context: Tabitha is an executive function coach. She helps neurodivergent students and their families build the skills and systems that support their academic and personal goals. ​ And she noticed something: ​ The challenge of getting started on a workout is almost identical to the challenge her students face when trying to start homework. ​ This might sound familiar. You get home after a long day, mentally fried, and all you want to do is veg out on the couch. ​ In that state, getting up to cook a healthy dinner or go do a workout can feel really freaking hard.

Switching from a “YEAH!” task (chilling on the couch) to a “NAH!” task (workout/homework), is often harder than the task itself.

If we can make that gear shift less dramatic, it can make a big difference!

Instead of going from YEAH! to NAH!, you insert at least one task that’s just…MEH.

If you’re struggling to start your workout, don’t fight the gear change. Bridge it.

Add a little MEH to the mix and see what happens.

Tabitha put together a free worksheet that walks you through mapping your own task initiation sequence. Your personal YEAH -> MEH -> NAH.

Try it this week, and keep me posted on how it goes. ​ You got this. ​ -Matt

2) Want a coach who builds a plan and walks with you each step of the way? Learn about NF Coaching.

#8789. Does Soreness Mean a Good Workout? No. Here’s What It Actually Tells You

Soreness is not an indicator of a good workout, and not being sore doesn’t mean your workout didn’t count.

That day-after ache (DOMS) mostly tells you that you did something new, not something effective.

Progress is more reliably measured in your training log: more weight, more reps, more control over time, sore or not.

Rachael (a reader and all-around amazing person) sent me a question about this so well-organized it came with multiple choice answers. 😃

I LOVE this question, because almost everyone who’s getting started (or starting again) wonders the same thing:

Quick definition first. That achy, stiff, “why does it hurt to sit on the toilet” feeling that shows up a day or two after a workout has a name: DOMS, or Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness.

It usually peaks somewhere around 24-72 hours after you train.

Severe soreness is NOT an indicator of a good workout.

It’s a sign that you did something new that your body isn’t used to yet:

But it’s also not something to be afraid of, especially if you switch up your routine and are mildly sore for a day or two.

Your body is adapting quickly! And as you adjust to the new exercises, you’ll be less and less sore from it.

So when is soreness helpful, if ever? ​ Soreness can give us a useful signal that we worked a muscle we were trying to target and hadn’t felt before.

But if you’re SUPER sore? Like, can’t get out of bed the next day and have to waddle around like a newborn giraffe sore? That’s a sign the jump was bigger than your body needed.

And the real cost (beyond the discomfort) is that it gets in the way of your next couple of workouts. Either because your technique gets sloppy because everything hurts, or you’re so wrecked that you don’t want to show up at all.

The best way to lower your odds of severe DOMS is to ease into a new program slowly.

Start with fewer sets and lighter weights than you think you need, and build from there. 💪

Yes! You DO need to push yourself over time in order to make progress:

That’s the law of progressive overload, and there’s no getting around it.

Sometimes adding that extra bit will make you sore. Other times, it won’t.

But it’s the underlying principle that matters: are you asking a little more of yourself over time? Not: did it hurt afterward?

So why do we care so much about soreness?

Here’s what I think we’ve fallen into with fitness in general.

We as humans operate really well with feedback. If we touch a hot stove, we get burned and know not to do that again.

We want to know, immediately after doing something, whether it worked or it didn’t.

And with strength training, you don’t feel stronger the next day. It takes time to build up.

So we reach for proxies that close that feedback loop.

It’s exactly like the story of minty toothpaste.

As the story goes, toothpaste manufacturers had a hard time selling their product until they added mint.

Suddenly, there was a tingly clean feeling you could latch onto. “Oh, this IS working.”

The mint doesn’t clean your teeth. But it’s associated with the thing that does, and it gave people something to feel.

It’s not the REASON you’re getting stronger.

But it can be associated with the work you do, especially as a beginner who is new to exercise, so we’ve learned to chase the tingle.

✅ How much weight, how many reps, how many sets are you doing?

✅ Do you feel more stable and controlled with the exercise than you did last month?

Then great! It’s working. Doesn’t matter if you never get sore.

And if you do end up super sore after trying something new, it’s not that you “failed”.

Just take it as a cue to introduce things more gently next time. 😊

So, back to Rachael’s multiple choice question.

C is really close. But I’ll add an fourth option:

D) Soreness tells you what was NEW. Your training log tells you what’s WORKING.

No extra fitness points for being sore. No points off if you do end up sore, either.

All the points gently ramping things up over time, and showing up again next time. 🔥

Is it bad if I’m never sore? No. If your weights, reps, or control are improving over time, your training is working, sore or not.

How long does DOMS last? It usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after the workout and fades over a few days. If you’re regularly wrecked for longer, ease the jumps in your program.

Should I work out while sore? Mild soreness is fine to train through, and easy movement often helps. If you’re severely sore, target a different part of the body, scale down, or take another rest day; what we don’t want to do is have sloppy technique because we’re SO sore we can’t perform the exercise normally.

#8788. Cold, Dark, Rainy? The 10 Best Editor-Tested Indoor Bike Trainers Keep Your Training on Track

Our editors tested the best indoor bike trainers for winter miles, Zwift rides, and every budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Well, friends, it’s that time of year again. Colder temperatures and shorter daylight hours mean indoor riding season is right around the corner for many of us—if it hasn’t already arrived where you live. But thankfully, newer trainer tech and digital connectivity make those boring nights spent staring at your basement wall or garage door while endlessly spinning the pedals a thing of the past.

Smart trainers—some priced under $500—connect to Zwift and Rouvy, popular platforms that feature virtual worlds, group rides, and even organized races. Plus, lower prices on nicely-equipped indoor bikes mean you no longer have to wrestle with putting your bike on the trainer or ruining pricey components with sweat.

Our editors test trainers year-round, from budget-friendly units to the most advanced smart bike models currently available. We do workouts and ride a ton of base miles; some staff even compete at a high level in virtual racing leagues, giving us important feedback on trainer accuracy, stability, and durability.

The Wahoo Kickr Core 2 with Zwift Cog and Click is our Best Overall Indoor Trainer because it’s the perfect choice for most riders. It combines Wahoo’s excellent base-model direct-drive trainer with Zwift’s singlespeed cog and virtual shifting. The system sets up easily and works with almost any bike, regardless of gear range or number of speeds. (You can easily swap the Zwift Cog with a cassette if you don’t like the virtual gearing.) This enables multiple riders in a household to share one trainer, even if their bikes have different drivetrains or gearing.

I used the first-generation Kickr Core as my home setup for four years without any issues. Wahoo’s recent updates to the Core only make an already great smart trainer even better. Test Editor Dan Chabanov recently used the new Kickr Core 2 for three months after switching from the more expensive Kickr V6. He said, “Honestly, I can’t say I’ve noticed any kind of downgrade.”

On paper, the Kickr Core 2 has lower maximum wattage, less grade simulation, and slightly less claimed accuracy. In practice, the ride feel is almost identical on both models. Like the Kickr V6, the Core now features Wi-Fi (along with Bluetooth and ANT+) for smooth connectivity and faster data transmission for online events. “Truly, the only reason to opt for the pricier V6 is that it folds slightly smaller and is easier to move around,” Chabanov concluded.

The Zwift Cog uses virtual shifting to change gears instead of your bike’s shifters and derailleurs. Unfortunately, virtual shifting only works in Zwift. If you plan to ride without Zwift (or on another platform), purchase the Kickr Core 2 with a cassette.

Tired of putting your bike on the trainer every time you want to ride indoors?

Dedicated training bikes, such as the Zwift Ride, are a great option for indoor riding. This way, you have a bike on the trainer that’s always ready to ride. No more fumbling to remove your wheel or wearing down tires. The Ride’s adjustment range also makes it easy to set up and share with multiple riders in a household.

“After more than a year of heavy use by my wife and me, the Zwift Ride has proven to be a durable, impressively quiet alternative to abusing our 'good' bikes on a trainer, with excellent Zwift integration and easy adjustability for our multi-rider household,” said Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips.

Zwift’s recent updates addressed our criticisms of the original Ride. The V2 now fits more riders (4’10” to 6’6”), adds saddle adjustability, and increases the bar diameter. It also includes Zwift’s multi-position crank with lengths from 160mm to 175mm, which used to be a $100 upcharge.

If you ride indoors and want a dedicated setup that integrates with Zwift out of the box (and don’t want to spend thousands of dollars for a premium indoor bike), the Zwift Ride is an excellent option. Zwift sells the Ride Smart Frame alone (without a trainer) for $800 if you already have a direct-drive trainer.

Since launching in 2012, the Wahoo Kickr has consistently been one of the best indoor trainers and a favorite of Bicycling’s staff. While the sixth version of the venerable smart trainer is more of an update than a wholesale redesign, the changes help the Kickr rank ahead of other high-performance smart trainers.

The latest iteration features the same flywheel as the previous one, so the two units look virtually identical. As a result, both generations experience the same ride feel. The Kickr ramps up smoothly and correctly as you accelerate. Power accuracy is very good, and most riders will find the claimed 1-percent accuracy to be true.

Despite its high price and lack of cassette-sizing options, the latest Kickr is a solid choice. It’s the best option for performance-minded cyclists who push big watts or racers who require accuracy and improved connectivity for online events.

If you need a basic, budget-friendly trainer that gets the job done in a pinch—and offers compatibility with third-party apps like Zwift—the Tacx Boost Trainer Bundle is a solid option. With its magnetic roller, you can manually adjust resistance across ten levels. And because the Boost uses magnetic resistance instead of fluid or fans, it stays relatively quiet. The loudest sounds you’ll hear are your drivetrain and the tire on the roller.

The bundle includes a Garmin speed sensor and a front wheel block to keep your bike level while riding. It also folds up easily for compact storage. For an easy-to-use, low-cost, no-frills setup, this one covers the essentials.

The Saris Fluid2 is a good trainer at a reasonable price. This makes it a solid pick for riders who need something basic to keep up with their training plan on rainy days, rehab from injury, or get back into riding before heading outside onto the bike path, road, or trails.

The Fluid2’s wheel-on design means you don’t need to fumble with your drivetrain to set it up, and the fluid resistance provides a smooth, progressive ride feel. Although this version isn’t compatible with Zwift, Rouvy, or other online platforms, the Saris combo kit (for $40 more) includes a wheel sensor that adds connectivity. Also be sure to get an adaptor kit if your bike has a thru axle rear wheel.

Instead of buying that no-name $50 or $80 trainer, spend a little more for a proven trainer from a trusted brand. While it looks similar to Saris’ Fluid 2 (above), the Mag Plus uses a magnetic sensor to provide resistance instead of fluid. This saves a little money and gives you a linear feel (versus the Fluid’s progressive resistance). However, a big downside is that they tend to wear out tires pretty quickly, especially pricey, high-performance rubber.

Mag trainers have been around for decades (I’ve had several from different brands over the years); the tech hasn’t changed much and they don’t have any smart features. If you plan to ride Zwift or Rouvy, you need to install a wheel sensor. If you need a super basic trainer that gets the job done for only $100, the Mag Plus is your best bet.

The Neo 3M matches the Wahoo Kickr in power measurement (up to 2,200 watts with 1% accuracy) and maximum simulated gradient (up to 25%), but it has two unique features. The Neo generates its own electricity, so you can use it without external power (though it works best when plugged in). And, like an old-school Nintendo Rumble Pack, the Neo 3M vibrates to simulate a wide range of road surfaces—from gravel to cobblestones to concrete slab roads—when you’re riding Zwift.

Unlike other direct-drive trainers that use belts or rollers to transmit power, the Neo 3M uses a metal flywheel with magnets that interact with electrical coils to moderate resistance. Combined with the built-in motion plates, the trainer has an impressively realistic ride feel. However, the Neo 3M lacks a native high-speed data transfer mode or built-in Wi-Fi—a great feature for competitive virtual racing—but Garmin offers a separate adaptor.

The Wahoo Kickr Bike Pro is the indoor trainer of choice for riders seeking the best possible experience—and who have the space for a dedicated setup. At $4,000, it’s like investing in an extra bike that you can’t even ride outside. However, for many riders, the price is worth it since it’s always ready to go. You don’t need to install a bike or connect any devices. Plus, highly corrosive sweat and salt from trainer rides won’t damage your outside bike.

The Kickr Bike Pro adjusts to almost all bike fit measurements. Or, if you had a Guru, Retül, or Trek bike fit, you can plug the dimensions into the Wahoo app for more precise setup. Since the Bike uses virtual shifting, you can program it to any Shimano, SRAM, or Campagnolo drivetrain you want to ride. You can select the gear ratios and the number of teeth per cog.

The Kickr Bike Pro’s incredible ride feel comes from its high-tech flywheel with motor; it adds resistance while simulating the inertia of real-world riding. The Pro provides a coasting feel along with realistic braking and shifting. The system also features a piston-like mechanism that reflects virtual elevation changes by adjusting the angle between the bike and the ground (up to 20% incline and 15% decline).

If the Kickr Bike Pro’s $4,000 price tag is a little out of reach, check out the Kickr Bike Shift. It’s similar to the Pro in adjustment, but ditched the fancy flywheel and gradient-change feature—and it saves you almost $1,500.

Feedback’s Omnium Over-Drive is compact, lightweight (14 pounds), and sets up and breaks down fast. That’s why these portable trainers are ubiquitous in parking lots and team tents at bike races. These same traits also make it a great option for riders with small apartments or training while away from home.

However, this portable trainer isn’t light on features. Two 4-inch magnetic drums provide progressive resistance up to 1,050 watts (at 55 mph). Thanks to its height-adjustable fork mount and sliding base, the Over-Drive accommodates most bikes, wheel sizes, and quick-release or thru-axle configurations. Feedback includes a durable tote bag for storage under a bed, in your garage, or in a car trunk.

The trainer’s compact size makes it easy to carry on a plane as checked luggage (or in your bike bag)—I brought it along many times on trips to Asia and Europe. Plus, the Omnium’s quiet ride won’t disturb neighbors in a hotel room.

Wahoo’s unique-looking Kickr Rollr is a novel approach to indoor trainers. It’s a great option for those who need to install or remove their bike quickly. This makes it easy to use in a pinch, such as when an afternoon thunderstorm rolls in and threatens to cancel your training ride.

At the front, the Rollr features an A-shaped bracket that holds your bike’s front wheel with a tool-free clamp that accommodates tires up to 2.1 inches/53mm wide. At the back, the Rollr’s two drums cradle your bike’s rear tire, and an external flywheel adds resistance.

This design makes it quick and easy to put a bike on the Kickr Rollr, swap out multiple bikes, or share a trainer with other riders. However, we don’t recommend this trainer for riders who do a lot of out-of-the-saddle, high-intensity training or for users who regularly race on Zwift. (A direct-drive trainer will be better suited for these tasks.)

While the Rollr is adjustable for different wheelbases, the adjustment is limited and optimized for road bikes. This means long-wheelbase mountain bikes might not fit (most road or gravel bikes shouldn’t have any issues). Since the trainer doesn’t read power, you must have a power meter to use the Rollr’s smart features.

Direct-drivetrainers attach to your bike’s rear dropouts and replace your rear wheel with a resistance unit. These trainers are typically quieter than other systems, provide more accurate power readings, and are ideal for high-power efforts.

Friction trainers use a roller pressed against your bike’s rear tire. They’re lighter, (usually) more affordable, and more portable than other systems. However, friction trainers can be very noisy and wear out tires.

Rollers are a time-tested indoor riding platform. They use three drums (rollers) that you ride on, so they require balance. While some rollers have resistance, many don’t.

Smart bikes are dedicated indoor training bikes. These trainers are heavy and take up space, but they’re a great option if you have a bigger budget, are tired of taking your bike on/off the trainer, or don’t want to wreck your outdoor bike with sweat and salt.

Typically, a smart trainer is an indoor trainer that can wirelessly communicate power data with a training app on a smartphone or computer. Most smart trainers also work with virtual riding platforms like Zwift by automatically adjusting resistance to simulate changes in terrain.

The popularity of online riding platforms means most newer trainers are “smart” and will both transmit your data and adjust resistance. These features often add to the cost of a new trainer. But prices are falling; you can find connected trainers—such as the Saris M2—for less than $200.

If you want to try Zwift but don’t have a smart trainer, you can still log virtual miles using a Bluetooth speed sensor. Check out our guide to getting started here.

Compatibility: With axle attachment standards and widths frequently changing, check if the trainer you want offers different attachment options (such as thru-axle adaptors, or for direct-attachment trainers, free-hub options). Some trainers come with them. If yours doesn’t, you’ll need to purchase them separately. The Robert Axle Project is my go-to resource for replacement thru-axles and adapters.

Noise: While most manufacturers can get away with using words like “silent” and “virtually silent” to describe the noise level of their trainers, there are other factors to consider, such as the sound your bike’s drivetrain makes as you pedal, and if you use one, the fan that’s whirring away to keep you cool and simulate wind speeds. To get a better idea of how loud “silent” actually is, we used a decibel meter to record the noise levels of each trainer being ridden at 15 and 25 mph. Decibels ranged from 68 (comparable to a vacuum cleaner) to 85 (a diesel truck going 40 mph); the fan alone measured 71. To get an idea of how significant a seemingly minor jump in decibels can be, 70 is twice as loud as 60, and 80 is twice as loud as 70.‌

Stability: Trainer crashes are rare, but not unheard of when you’re going cross-eyed trying to beat your PR on a workout. Typically, the wider the trainer’s base, the more stable it will be. Many have a leveling feature for uneven surfaces.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#8787. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

#8786. How Fast Do You Actually Lose Strength? Slower Than You Think

You lose strength much more slowly than you probably think.

A few days off changes basically nothing, measurable losses take roughly two to four weeks depending on the quality (muscle endurance fades first, maximal strength last).

Muscle memory makes rebuilding faster than building the first time, and maintaining takes a fraction of the training that building did.

Here’s the timeline, and how it can inform your training.

Has this question ever crossed your mind:

This was an awesome question that Charles sent my way. (Thanks Charles! 🙌)

When life gets crazy and you find yourself skipping workouts, there’s a voice that says:

I had that exact thought the first time I had to take significant time away for a back injury.

And heck, just recently my kiddos brought home the “crud” from school and I missed a full week of workouts.

So, let’s look at what actually happens, and what it means for your training.

Short version: a few days off doesn’t impact your maximum strength or muscle size basically at all.

Your muscles may look or feel “flatter”, but that’s because stored water and glycogen decrease, not because you are weaker.

And this “pump” comes back quickly once you start training again. 💪

Here’s a rough timeline of when we start to see the effects of detraining:

Highly trained folks and older adults will notice detraining faster than new or younger lifters (so they’ll sit towards the beginning of these timelines.)

But you don’t lose your progress in any meaningful way after a week or 2 away from the gym. 😊

And if you DO have to spend significant time away for whatever reason, I have good news for you, too:

1) Your nervous system remembers how to do the movement.

The first session or two in the gym after time away may feel a bit clunky, but you’ll quickly regain the technique.

And a big component of strength is neuromuscular coordination (i.e. your brain and muscles firing together more efficiently, which improves rapidly.)

2) The muscle itself seems to hold onto some of the machinery it built, so it rebuilds faster the second time.

A general rule of thumb is about 50% as long as you were away (so if you were away for 12 weeks, it may take ~6 weeks to rebuild your strength.) Take this with a grain of salt as there is a LOT of variation here. This isn’t a hard and fast rule.

(And you don’t want to jump right back in at 100%. Use the 50/50 rule to get yourself going again.)

The point is, it’s generally easier to rebuild than to build the first time.

Building muscle and strength? It takes time and effort.

No one wakes up a day after a workout and has just magically put on 5 pounds of muscle.

That takes only a fraction of the volume.

When you keep intensity the same (i.e. how hard the exercise is), doing 1/3 the number of sets maintains your strength for a loooong time. ​ The point being: doing ANYTHING during a period where you aren’t able to consistently work out is still really really helpful!

When life throws you off track with your fitness goals, you’re not starting back from square zero.

And even a single session each week with a couple challenging sets is enough to hold what you’ve built until things calm down.

There’s that old saying that: “The best time to invest was 20 years ago. The next best time to invest is today.”

I think the same holds true for building up your fitness.

Every session you put in now is strength you get to keep later.

This is exactly why we built our coaching program. Because having a coach makes both of those so much smoother. ​ We take the thinking off your plate so it’s easier to get going.

We direct your limited time and effort toward the stuff that actually moves the needle. ​ AND when life pulls you away (sick kids, a work deadline, etc.) we help you maintain and get right back at it. ​ If that sounds like the kind of help you’ve been looking for, here’s how NF Coaching works. 💪 ​ -Matt

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

#8785. Replacing Your Bike Chain Is Easier Than You Think—Here’s How to Do It at Home

A step-by-step home repair guide to measuring, removing, and installing a bike chain.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Replacing a chain is a great way for someone to tap into their home bike maintenance potential. It’s a pretty straightforward process once you’re used to it, especially if you have the existing chain to measure from. I typically recommend being familiar with a few skills before diving into replacing your chain. The first skill to know is adjusting your front and rear derailleurs. The second is knowing how to use a chain checker. The third is being familiar with a pre bike check. This last one is especially helpful because it will allow you to run through the bike to see if there are any other issues before diving into swapping out your chain. Again, these skills are not required skills to replace a chain, but having some familiarity with the basic mechanics addressed above will only help make this process easier. Here we’ll go through the tools you’ll need and the basic process to replace your chain at home.

How often should you replace your chain? Before answering that question, it helps to understand the process of chain wear. As your chain ages, each link’s internal bushings slowly lengthen. In turn, your now-longer chain puts added pressure on your cassette cogs and chainring teeth, causing them to wear faster. This also hampers shifting quality.

To avoid this accelerated wear of your cassette and chainrings, a general rule of thumb is to replace your bike’s chain every 2,000 miles. Mind you, this is just a starting point. No two chains will wear at exactly the same rate because no two riders treat their chains the same.

These differences in riding style are why it is best to periodically use a chain wear measuring tool to determine the condition of your chain. With the tool in hand, apply pressure to a pedal so the top of the chain is taut, and then place the measuring tool in place on the chain as shown in the video above and read the results. Indicators on the tool will tell you whether it’s time to replace your chain.

Cutting a new bike chain to the correct length for installation and removing a damaged link for an on-trail chain repair are essentially the same job. Make life easier by using a full-size tool at home, and save the compact tool for midride fixes.

To start, you’ll need to pick up the right size chain for your bike. We’re not talking about the length of the chain here (you’ll address that later), but width. This is dictated by the number of cogs on your cassette; a six-speed bike uses the same width chain as an eight-speed, but a nine-speed needs something different, and so on. (Check out Park Tool’s chain compatibility guide for more on this.) The easiest way to ensure you get the right chain is to buy the same kind of chain that came on your bike. If you decide to go with a different chain, it’s best to get one from the same manufacturer.

If your chain has a master link such as a Shimano Quick Link or SRAM PowerLock, use a pair of master link pliers to compress the link and undo it. (If it’s a newer chain, you might be able to do this with your hands.)

If there isn’t a master link, remove the chain using the chain breaker tool. Back out the tool’s pin to make room and fit a chain link into the outer slot, and line up the tool’s pin with a pin on the chain. Tighten the tool until its pin puts light pressure on the chain’s connecting pin. Crank the handle, making sure the tool’s pin stays straight. If it twists, stop and realign everything so as not to bend the tool’s pin. If you bend it, most tools have replaceable pins available; some even come with one inside the handle. Then push the pin far enough through so you can remove the extra links.

Remove the chain from your bike. Then, measure out the length of your new chain to match the length of your old chain, taking into account the master link. Remove any excess links from the new chain using the chain breaker tool, and install the master link. Thread the new chain onto your bike’s cassette and chainring and connect the ends with the master link, making sure the link is secure and locked in place.

When she’s not out riding her mountain bike, Jessica is an editor for Popular Mechanics. She was previously an editor for Bicycling magazine.

A will (technically a "last will and testament") is a legal document that specifies how your assets should be distributed after your death. It must go through probate — a court-supervised process that validates the will, pays debts and taxes, and distributes assets to beneficiaries. A living trust (specifically a revocable living trust) is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. When you die, the successor trustee distributes those assets according to the trust terms — without court involvement.

You need both: A trust does not name guardians for minor children (only a will can do that), and a trust only controls assets that have been formally transferred into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — it directs any assets not in the trust at your death to pour into the trust, where they are distributed according to the trust terms. The pour-over will still goes through probate, but it ensures nothing falls through the cracks.

The term "living trust" almost always refers to a revocable living trust — one you can change, amend, or dissolve at any time during your lifetime. You remain the trustee, manage the assets as you always have, and pay taxes on trust income using your personal Social Security number. For income tax purposes, a revocable trust is invisible — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist.

An irrevocable trust is fundamentally different. Once established, you cannot easily modify it, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. This permanence provides two powerful advantages:

The federal estate tax exemption is $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples) in 2026, but this historically high exemption is scheduled to sunset after 2025, potentially dropping to approximately $7 million per person. FIRE households who have built $3 million to $10 million in net worth through decades of saving and investment growth should monitor this sunset closely. If the exemption drops, irrevocable trusts become relevant at much lower wealth levels.

For most FIRE households with $1 million to $5 million in net worth, a revocable living trust provides the right balance of control, flexibility, and probate avoidance. Irrevocable structures become compelling only when estate tax exposure is real or asset protection needs are elevated.

Estate planning is governed primarily by state law, and the value of a living trust versus a will varies significantly depending on where you live.

Nine states are community property states: Arizona, California, Idaho, Louisiana, Nevada, New Mexico, Texas, Washington, and Wisconsin. In these states, most assets acquired during marriage are owned 50/50 by both spouses regardless of whose name is on the title. At death, only the deceased spouse's half passes through their estate plan.

The remaining 41 states follow common law (also called "equitable distribution"). Ownership depends on whose name is on the title. This distinction affects how assets pass at death and whether a trust or will provides better spousal protection.

Use this framework to determine whether you need a trust, a will, or both:

A revocable living trust is strongly recommended if:

Remember that a trust only controls assets titled in the trust's name. After creating a trust, you must fund it by re-titling your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust. Unfunded trusts — trusts that exist on paper but hold no assets — provide zero benefit. The pour-over will catches stragglers, but relying entirely on the pour-over defeats the purpose because those assets still go through probate.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common estate planning mistake with trusts is failing to fund them. Creating a trust document costs $1,500 to $5,000, but if you never transfer your bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate into the trust, it provides zero probate avoidance. After signing your trust, immediately re-title assets into the trust name. Your attorney should provide a funding checklist. An unfunded trust sitting in a drawer is an expensive piece of paper — not an estate plan.

Yes. A pour-over will catches any assets not transferred into your trust during your lifetime and directs them into the trust at death. A will is also the only legal document that can name guardians for minor children. Every trust-based estate plan should include a pour-over will.

A revocable living trust prepared by an estate planning attorney typically costs $1,500 to $5,000, depending on complexity and your location. This usually includes the trust document, pour-over will, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and initial funding guidance. Online trust services cost $200 to $500 but may not address state-specific issues or complex situations.

Yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as both the grantor (creator) and the trustee (manager). You maintain full control over all trust assets during your lifetime. You name a successor trustee who takes over only if you become incapacitated or die.

A revocable living trust does not reduce estate taxes — the IRS treats it as if it does not exist for income and estate tax purposes. However, a trust can be structured with provisions (such as an A/B trust or disclaimer trust) that maximize the use of both spouses' estate tax exemptions. For estate tax reduction, irrevocable trusts are the primary tool.

A revocable trust can be changed, amended, or dissolved at any time. You maintain full control. An irrevocable trust generally cannot be changed after creation, and the assets inside it are no longer legally yours. Revocable trusts provide probate avoidance and incapacity planning. Irrevocable trusts provide estate tax reduction and asset protection.

Without a trust, each state where you own real property requires a separate probate proceeding (called ancillary probate), multiplying costs and complexity. Transferring out-of-state property into a living trust eliminates ancillary probate entirely — the successor trustee can transfer or sell the property without court involvement in any state.

#8782. Why You Keep Falling Off Your Fitness Routine (and the 2-Minute Plan That Fixes It)

Expecting yourself to stick to the same fitness routine, no matter what, is why it fails.

Because the only predictable thing about life is that it’s unpredictable.

A kid gets sick. Sleep falls apart. The to-do list explodes.

You can’t know which one is coming or when, but you can know something is, and you can build your routine to expect it.

That’s the whole trick: take two minutes and decide, in advance, exactly what you’ll do the next time life goes sideways.

Here’s the coaching conversation that shows how it works.

I want to let you in on one of my biggest lessons from the last 15 years of coaching.

Once you know it, it will feel like you can see the future. 👀

On a live Q&A, George (not his real name) told me about a pattern he kept running into.

Then a kiddo would get sick, or some other responsibility would pop up, sleep would fall apart for a bit, and the whole routine would go with it.

And he got this look like “Oooooohhhhhhhh…no. No I haven’t.”

He’d been treating the sick kid as something that happens to the plan.

So we talked through it right there. Here’s what we came up with:

Now, he wasn’t just reacting in the moment, trying to “gut it out.”

He knew exactly what to do and it fit what he needed.

Here’s the thing: these moments don’t come out of the blue. They are predictable.

You’ll have WAY too much on your to-do list.

I don’t know which one, or when exactly, but I do know that it’s inevitable.

Once we accept that the only predictable thing is that life is unpredictable, we can use that to our advantage.

Take two minutes right now and finish this sentence:

First blank: the thing that knocked you off track the last time you were trying to get into a fitness routine.

Second blank: the best version of your plan you can still commit to on one of THOSE days.

Sometimes, life will throw something at you that you REALLY didn’t see coming.

But the more of these you’ve been through, the clearer the crystal ball becomes.

And the better you get at navigating it. 💪

Hit reply and send me your crystal ball plan. I read every one, and I’ll tell you if I’d tweak it.

-Matt ​ ​P.S. This is exactly the type of stuff we work on in our coaching program. My job as your coach is to look into my crystal ball, and help you plan ahead so you don’t get blindsided. 🔮👀 Learn more about how coaching works [HERE].

#8781. Menopause and mental health: The science of the menopausal brain

Reviewed by Brian St. Pierre, MS, RD and Helen Kollias, PhD

On a Friday night, as my husband and I tried to figure out where to eat, a typical conversation would go like this:

Me: Do you want to go to that restaurant?

Me: I can’t think of the name. We’ve eaten there before. It’s that place with the peanut shells on the floor? It’s next to… You know… It’s on that road where we used to take the dog to the vet. Do you know the one I’m talking about??

It was as if certain details got lost in a pile of sludge in the deep recesses of my brain. Then, hours later, the details would escape, and I’d shout into an empty room…

However, what seemed to be happening to me, increasingly in my late 40s and early 50s, felt far from typical.

Not only could I never seem to spit out the names of various restaurants or people or books or movies or so many other things, but my brain was also pooping out during the workday.

I’d sit in front of my computer screen, stare at a document, and will myself to do something constructive with my fingertips. Everything seemed hazy, like those first few moments in the morning when you’re awake enough to turn off the alarm but too sleepy to do basic math.

I had my good moments, usually in the morning, when I attempted to pack eight hours of writing into the two or three hours I possessed mental clarity.

On my worst days, however, I awoke with a haze I never managed to shake. Work was a non-starter. Nor did I have enough bandwidth to read, or do much of anything, really.

Three healthcare professionals recommended antidepressants. I tried one, and felt even worse. I tried another. I tried yet another at a higher dose. Still, I felt like a zombie. Another professional gave me a sleeping pill. It left me feeling even more drugged.

Someone tested my thyroid. There was nothing wrong with it. Nor was I anemic. I tried supplements, mushroom coffee, and just about any product with the word “think” somewhere on its label.

Finally, after nearly two years of seeing a revolving door of doctors, I made an appointment with a gynecologist for my yearly exam. I mentioned vaginal dryness. That information triggered her to ask a string of questions that had nothing to do with my undercarriage. How was my sleep? Mood? Energy levels? Was I experiencing hot flashes? How about brain fog?

“Funny you should mention brain fog,” I said in my usual hazy monotone. “I feel like I’m barely alive.”

By the end of the visit, I understood that I’d likely never had depression.

My gynecologist sent me home with prescriptions for estradiol and progesterone.

Within days, it was as if someone had flipped a switch.

I could think again. I could type words again. I could follow conversations. I could work past noon.

And, for the first time in years, I could sleep more than two hours without waking.

Here’s your sign. The Nutrition Coach Starter Package combines the world’s #1 nutrition certification with practical business tools to help you find clients and grow. Early Black Friday pricing, available now.

Instead, like puberty, it’s a life stage—a transitional moment to be precise.

Once you’ve gone 12 consecutive months without a period, you’ve reached menopause. And from that moment onwards, you’re officially “postmenopausal.”

As women approach this transitional moment, hormone levels fluctuate and fall, triggering dozens of symptoms. Weight gain and reduced sex drive get a lot of attention.

However, during and after menopause, roughly 40 percent of women report increased irritability, mood swings, anxiety, fatigue, and trouble concentrating, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.1 2 As the following image shows, it’s also one of the most vulnerable times in a woman’s life to develop depression,3 particularly if they’ve struggled in the past with it before.

Before starting hormones, I often found myself sobbing for no reason. Other times, the world’s stimuli felt too… stimulating.

Normal everyday sounds—like the buzz of traffic or people at the mall—literally hurt. I was jumpy and irritable and felt anxious about situations that had never bothered me in the past, such as driving over bridges or through construction.

Fluctuating hormone levels likely play a role, as do typical age-related changes in the brain.

In addition, during this stage of life, women often deal with several issues that siphon cognitive capacity faster than a thirsty vampire drains a carotid.

During their 40s and 50s, for example, many women have reached the peak of their careers, with responsibilities that follow them home and keep them up at night. They may also be parenting angst-filled teens, caring for aging parents, adjusting to an empty nest, questioning their marriage, or trying to wrap their bank account around the latest statement from the college bursar or hospital billing department.

However, one of the lesser-known and talked about triggers for cognitive discontent has nothing to do with aging or life stress and everything to do with that hallmark menopausal symptom: the hot flash.

Hot flashes, which happen during the day, and night sweats, which occur at night, fall under the category of vasomotor symptoms. (The word “vasomotor” refers to the constriction or dilation of blood vessels which, in turn, can influence everything from blood pressure to sweating.)

During a hot flash or night sweat, norepinephrine and cortisol levels rise. Blood vessels dilate in an attempt to shed heat. Blood pressure and heart rate increase.

Depending on the severity of the hot flash, your skin might redden as sensations of warmth spread through your face, neck, and chest.

You might sweat, experience heart palpitations, or feel anxious, tired, or faint.4

It’s not entirely clear why hot flashes crop up around menopause.

According to one theory, falling estrogen levels affect the hypothalamus, the area of the brain involved in temperature regulation. The brain’s internal thermostat gets wonky and occasionally thinks your body is too hot or cold (when it’s not).

For many years, experts thought of vasomotor symptoms as mere inconveniences or sources of embarrassment.

(To be honest, so did I. During all of those fruitless visits to various healthcare professionals, it never occurred to me to mention them.)

However, an increasing body of research has revealed that hot flashes may do more than make us uncomfortable or force us to change our sheets in the middle of the night.

They may also affect our blood vessels and brains—and not for the better.5 For this reason, an increasing number of experts now consider vasomotor symptoms to be a treatable medical condition.6 7 8

In one study, researchers asked 226 women to wear monitors that tracked when they were experiencing a hot flash. The women also underwent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), filled out sleep diaries, and wore smartwatches that recorded how often they woke at night.9

As researchers looked at the brain images obtained from women who experienced the most hot flashes, they noticed an abundance of patchy areas called whole-brain white matter intensities.

These lesions were once thought of as a typical consequence of aging. However, neuroscientists now believe that the presence of whole-brain white matter intensities is predictive of future cognitive decline.

People with an abundance of these brain lesions are twice as likely to get diagnosed with dementia and three times as likely to have a future stroke.10

It’s thought that the increased presence of whole-brain white matter intensities may stem, in part, from changes taking place in the blood vessels that feed the brain.

A three-year study of 492 women supports that theory. It determined that women who experienced frequent hot flashes also tended to experience unhealthy changes in their blood vessels, such as an inability to dilate to accommodate increased blood flow.11

Other research has linked frequent hot flashes with increases in the following:

In addition to directly affecting the blood vessels, frequent hot flashes may also affect the brain by disturbing sleep.17

Interestingly, many women don’t necessarily know that hot flashes are disturbing their sleep.

They may instead—as I did—assume they have insomnia or sleep apnea.

That’s because night sweats aren’t always sweaty.

By the time a surge in cortisol and norepinephrine jolts a woman awake, the hotness of the flash may have dissipated. So, it can feel as if she’s repeatedly waking, over and over and over again, for no discernable reason.

These frequent awakenings may interfere with the brain’s ability to consolidate memories, metabolize toxins, and store all the names, dates, and facts one encounters daily.

It can also lead to lost connectivity in the hippocampus, a part of the brain that’s important for learning and memory.

Sleep loss also means the amygdala, a part of the brain involved in emotion, becomes more reactive, causing people to feel more easily stressed, anxious, irritable, frustrated, or enraged.18 19

All of these brain changes can set in after just days to a week of lost sleep. So, imagine what happens when you’ve been waking over and over again—for years.

To diagnose depression, healthcare professionals use a tool called the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) depression scale. If you check off four of the nine symptoms on the scale, you’re considered depressed.

However, four of the symptoms on the checklist also overlap with the symptoms of menopause-related sleep deprivation:

Check off those four items, and you might be diagnosed with depression, even if what’s really ailing you is the battle with sleep you’ve been waging since you turned 47.

Another problem: On surveys, 80 percent of medical residents admit they feel “barely comfortable” talking about menopause.20 In addition, few residency programs—including ob-gyn residency programs—offer training in it.21

Given the above, it’s no wonder so many healthcare professionals never think to ask about hot flashes or sleep disturbances when people like me show up complaining of fatigue, lack of gumption, and an inability to focus.

In addition, even when it’s clear that vasomotor symptoms are leading to cognitive and emotional symptoms, many healthcare professionals still shy away from prescribing menopausal hormone therapy (also called hormone replacement therapy, or HRT), often telling women that supplemental hormones are “not safe” or “too risky.”

These professionals are practicing what Michigan-based menopause-trained gynecologist Jerrold H. Weinberg, MD, calls “defensive medicine.”

“It’s one of the first reflexes doctors have when they recommend a treatment,” says Dr. Weinberg. “They worry they’re going to get sued.”

These worries are based on research done several decades ago that linked the use of certain types of hormones with a slightly increased risk of developing breast cancer or stroke.22

However, according to more recent research, that small increased risk seems to depend on several other factors, such as age, dose, the type of hormonal preparation, and the duration of hormone use.23 24

As long as you’re younger than 60 and have been postmenopausal for fewer than 10 years, many experts now say the benefits outweigh the risks for women with moderate to severe menopausal symptoms.25

It’s also counterbalanced by health benefits such as reduced risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease or osteoporosis, says Dr. Weinberg, who confirms the health benefits of menopause hormone therapy far outweigh the risks for most women.

Because some antidepressants can lift mood, improve sleep, and reduce hot flashes, some healthcare professionals turn to them instead of menopause hormone therapy. As with any medicine, antidepressants have their own list of side effects. However, for someone practicing defensive medicine, they often seem like a safer bet, says Dr. Weinberg.26 27 28

If you or your client are on what seems like a never-ending quest to find a healthcare professional who understands menopause, use the following advice from Dr. Weinberg and Helen Kollias, PhD, an expert on physiology and molecular biology and science advisor at Precision Nutrition and Girls Gone Strong.

▶ Seek care from a menopause-trained health professional.

Usually, these professionals list this training and interest in their bio. For example, they might list “menopause” as an area of focus.

You can also search this database for practitioners who have earned a certification from the Menopause Society.

Write them down. That way, if you feel foggy or nervous during your appointment, you can lean on your notes.

This information can also help you judge whether MHT or another medicine is working. Based on your symptom data, you and your healthcare professional may decide to switch to a different medicine or change your dose.

▶ Be as specific as you can during your appointment.

Saying something like “I don’t sleep well,” is less likely to get you the right kind of help than saying, “During the past seven days, I’ve only gotten four uninterrupted hours once. I wake, on average, five times a night. On a typical night, my longest stretch of sleep is three hours.”

If you use a smartwatch, come ready to fire up your health app, so your healthcare professional can see the data.

▶ Talk about the pros and cons of treatment.

There’s a concept in medicine known as “shared decision-making.” Part of that process involves frank discussions about the benefits and risks of a given treatment. Then, patients and clinicians work together to make decisions based on those benefits and risks.

Many healthcare networks encourage clinicians to use shared decision-making, as it seems to reduce patient complaints as well as malpractice lawsuits.29 30

For this reason, shared decision-making can help shift a healthcare professional out of the “defensive medicine” mindset.

The lifestyle habits that improve mental and emotional health during menopause aren’t terribly different from the lifestyle habits that improve overall health—for any person, at any stage of life.

Other than avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and spicy or hot foods, there’s no special diet for people with vasomotor symptoms. (And by the way, tofu and other soy products don’t seem to help with vasomotor symptoms as much as once thought30—though they’re still nutritious.)

Healthy behaviors don’t necessarily change during middle age.

Nutrition, physical activity, stress management, sleep, social connectedness, and a sense of purpose matter just as much during the menopausal transition as they do when we’re younger. However, these fundamentals are even more important to dial in as life progresses.

If you answered “no” to some or all of those questions, consider why that is. What’s stopping you? How might you remove barriers or shore up support to make those fundamentals easier?

In addition to helping to blunt age- and hormone-related losses in muscle and bone mass, creatine may also help bolster mood and brain function while reducing mental fatigue.

It also seems to counter some of the negative effects of sleep deprivation. 32 33 Research shows a daily dose of 5 to 7 grams of creatine monohydrate is effective.

In addition to helping you feel alert, sunlight helps to set the internal clock in your brain that makes you sleepy at night and spunky in the morning. Morning and late afternoon light exposure seem particularly potent.

In a study of 103 people, exposure to morning sunlight predicted better sleep quality the following night. When people spent time outdoors in the mornings, they fell asleep more quickly, slept longer, and experienced fewer awakenings the following evening.34

Sunlight may also improve mood and concentration.35

If you’re already worn out, long, intense exercise sessions will likely make you feel worse.

For one, injuries crop up much more easily at middle age than during our 20s and 30s. In addition, it takes longer to recover between sessions.36

String too many overly zealous workouts too close together, and you’ll not only likely start to feel achy but also more irritable, tense, and tired.

However, much like a cold shower, short bursts of exercise may help you to feel alert during the day.

If you’re falling asleep at your desk, encourage yourself to take short movement breaks such as a 5- or 10-minute walk outdoors or a quick set of pushups or squats.

In addition, you may find gentle exercise—such as yoga or stretching—helps you relax before bed. Just don’t make it too intense, or you’ll trigger a release of adrenaline.

Whenever you exercise, tune into how your body feels, especially after a particularly bad night of sleep.

We’re not saying you should never exercise vigorously or try to beat your lifting PRs. However, depending on your sleep and recovery, you might want to pare things back, especially if you’ve traditionally hit the gym hard.

You can still do intense sessions—just balance them out with more moderate sessions, as well as proportionate recovery.

Depending on how you feel, you might decide to go all out, as usual.

However, you might also decide to do a zone 2 training session instead of an intense run. Or, if you’re resistance training, you might still do your planned session, but reduce the number of sets, reps, or volume lifted.

This research-based therapy for insomnia can help you develop skills and mental reframes that encourage sound sleep.

For example, a CBT-I therapist will help you develop the skill of getting up at the same time every day, regardless of how badly you slept (or didn’t sleep) the night before.

(Read more: Three CBT-I skills that can transform how you sleep.)

You may not have the energy (or desire) to do everything you did when you were younger. (When you were 36, your daily checklist defied time and space.)

As a result, you might benefit from looking critically at your current responsibilities to see which ones you can shrink or downsize. For several days, track how you spend your time and bandwidth. Then, analyze your data.

If you’re a coach, use the Wheel of Stress Assessment to help clients identify different dimensions of their life that might be draining their mental and emotional capacity. (When you know specifically where your stress is coming from, you have a better chance of resolving it.)

If it’s demands from other people that prevent you from prioritizing self-care and recovery, you might like to read: How saying “no” can seriously change your life.

You might find you sleep better and experience fewer night sweats if you sleep in a cooler environment.

Try turning down the thermostat a couple of degrees, using a fan, or investing in an electric cooling mattress pad.

When you feel the fog take over your brain, it’s not likely you’ll be doing “your best work” anyway.

So, for a block of time—say, 20 minutes—permit yourself to do nothing. You might:

If you need a quick “refresh,” you can also try a 5-minute mind-body scan.

Get your body into a comfortable position. For example, you might use the yoga “legs up the wall” pose or lie down and place a pillow under your knees.

Then, close your eyes and bring your attention to physical sensations in your body. Start at your head, and work your way down to your toes.

Don’t judge or rush to change anything. Just observe, like a scientist. You can also scan your mind, for example, by noticing thoughts.

When you’ve completed the scan, consider:

You don’t have to “do” anything with the information you uncover, just notice.

The foods that protect the blood vessels around your heart can also protect the blood vessels in your brain.

For example, both the MIND and Mediterranean diets are associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer’s disease and depression.37 38 These eating patterns are rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, olives, beans, fish, and other minimally-processed whole foods.

In addition, nitrate-rich foods like beets and dark, leafy greens may help to dilate blood vessels, temporarily improving memory by helping more blood to reach the brain.39 40

(For more on how our diet can support brain function and emotional regulation, read: Nutrition and mental health: What (and how) to eat)

It’s frustrating when you feel like you can’t do it all.

However, this stage of life presents a hidden opportunity, forcing you to re-evaluate what’s most important.

Before going on hormones, as my ability to type coherent words and phrases diminished, I was forced to ask an important question:

It was more of an existential question than a career-related one, and it allowed me to reassess how I wanted to spend my limited mental resources.

Given that I was self-employed, I didn’t actually need to be working eight hours a day. That was a gift, wasn’t it?

Maybe I also didn’t need to cook dinner six nights out of seven. Maybe the recipes I chose could be simplified, too.

Finally, maybe saying “no” a lot more often and without regret would allow me to continue to say yes to the things that mattered most.

And picking up the phone whenever my kid called from college.

Or meeting a friend for a meandering walk around town.

Thanks to the hormones and life tweaks, I now have energy again. I’m also clear-headed most of the time. However, I still tend to end my work day around 3 p.m.

#8780. I Rode My Bike in a Climate Chamber That Can Recreate Almost Any Weather on the Planet—Here’s My Biggest Takeaway

Inside Italy’s Terra X Cube, a Tour de France simulation became a real-world heat test.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I looked into the giant chamber filled with strategically placed bike trainers and couldn’t help but question what I signed up for. The chamber we were walking into is called the Terra X Cube located in Bolzano, Italy, and is designed to replicate conditions from anywhere on the planet. The chamber can recreate a snowstorm on Mount Everest or a heat wave in the Sahara.

Variables like temperature, humidity, wind, precipitation, and altitude can all be controlled from a small observation room just one door over. I knew immediately when I crossed into the threshold of the chamber and the heat hit me in the face that this would be a rough trainer ride.

I was in Bolzano, Italy for an opportunity to participate in this testing in the Terra X Cube as well as tour the apparel brand Q36.5’s headquarters based in Bolzano. The apparel from Q36.5 quickly became my top choice for cycling apparel after getting the chance to test some pieces from their kit for the last few months. Our hot and humid summer in the Northeast gave a perfect testing ground for the Q36.5 Dottore jersey and bibs—and they shined. When a chance to learn more about this brand by visiting their Italian headquarters came up, I jumped on a plane—the opportunity to experience riding in a climate chamber was a special bonus.

Here I’m going to talk about the unique experience of riding in a climate chamber with the heat turned up and my biggest takeaway that you can apply to your trainer riding this season.

The test course and climate were designed to replicate the last section of Stage 2 from the 2026 men’s Tour de France ending in Barcelona. We rode with a custom workout in Zwift and our data was being tracked across the board: SRM cranks to track power, heart rate data to validate fatigue, and CORE sensors to track our heat strain throughout the workout. The room was set to a balmy 97 degrees Fahrenheit.

There was even a tester from Q36.5 in the room with us with a custom jersey. The jersey he wore was effectively two jerseys cut in half at the zipper and straight down the back. He had multiple CORE heat sensors attached around his body to track which jersey design and material was more effective at thermoregulation. One of those jersey designs will end up in a future product.

The ride was supposed to last for about 45 minutes, but our group was the first of the day and ran into some technical difficulties getting the trainers set up. In one sense this was good because we were able to have an extended warmup on the trainers, but the reality meant we spent an extra 45 minutes warming up in the already heated up chamber.

Thankfully, over the last few months, I’ve been doing heat training protocols with my CORE training sensor. I dove straight in with six weeks of active heat training, then I pivoted to strictly passive heat training with my home sauna. While I was absolutely heating up I was relatively comfortable rolling into the ride.

Once we got through our extended warmup we began the proper ride. Effectively we were shooting for an over-under workout that emulated the end of stage two at this year’s Tour de France. I had my CORE temperature data up on the screen and saw that before we were starting the ride my internal temperature was at about 99 degrees. The giant fans at the front of the room would change power to replicate the airflow during climbs versus descents, but at those temperatures it felt like sitting in front of a massive hair dryer.

As we began the official warmup my temperature steadily climbed—according to my CORE sensor I peaked just over 102 degrees. In the middle of the test I looked around the room and everyone looked like they were putting out high effort, even when we were supposed to be sitting in our recovery phase. The heat was taking its toll and our views did not inspire a boost in energy. Staring at the metallic walls while pedaling on our hamster wheel bikes did not give inspiration for an extra push for our final sprint. But as we finished up our not-so-cool cooldown I couldn’t help but think I would do it again.

After our group left the chamber the second group queued up for their turn on the bikes. The technical difficulties were overcome with our group, so they were able to jump straight into the ride after a five-minute warmup. That night we all regrouped to go through the data and we were able to see our data versus the data from some of the professionals in the stage we recreated. My biggest takeaway from the comparison to the professionals was their core temperature data. The professionals we were comparing against showed very little heat strain compared to even the fittest in our group. It’s worth noting the professionals had also already ridden over 60 miles before our route even started—those professionals were extremely heat adapted.

My biggest personal takeaway was how I could recreate this at home. When I talked to someone else in my group we discussed the similarities to this experience and heat training at home. When I do an active heat session at home I layer up in three layers top and bottom, a painter’s suit with the shins and feet cut off (so it doesn’t get caught in the cranks), and a hat or beanie for good measure. My active heat session numbers at home are surprisingly similar to this experience: typically a 45-minute warmup gets me into zone three of the heat strain index in the CORE app and then I spend about 45 minutes in this zone. This shows you don’t need a massive climate chamber to get the training benefits of heat training. Some warm layers, a painter’s suit, a CORE sensor, and a bike trainer can give you the benefits you need to develop this component of training.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
