#8688. The Best Protein Powders for Weight Loss, According to a Certified Nutrition Coach

Protein powder can help you maintain muscle mass while eating in a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and found nine we think are best for weight loss.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Feb 19, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

When someone says they want to lose weight, what they really mean is they want to shed excess body fat. However, without a well-designed plan in place, a calorie deficit leads you to lose both fat and valuable muscle tissue. To minimize muscle loss, it’s crucial to incorporate resistance training, quality sleep, and a high-protein diet into your regular routine.

Protein plays a multifaceted role in weight management, influencing factors like hunger levels, metabolism, and muscle preservation. While heavy resistance training provides the necessary stimulus, signaling to the body that existing muscle should be retained, a high-protein diet ensures the body has an ample supply of amino acids. This prevents your body from metabolizing muscle tissue for energy.

The best protein powders provide a convenient and lean source of the muscle-building macronutrient, helping you hit your daily protein goals while also maintaining a calorie deficit. We tested more than 100 protein powders and selected nine products we think are best for weight loss.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

We chose these products based on a number of factors, including:

I chose Transparent Labs as the best protein powder for weight loss because it has a very high ratio of protein to the total number of calories: 28 grams to 130 calories. This helps you maximize protein consumption during a caloric deficit, which helps prevent you from losing muscle while you’re losing weight. It’s also third-party tested, Informed Choice certified, and completely artificial ingredient-free. And it comes in 15 flavor options.

I’ve tried a number of different flavors from Transparent Labs and Chocolate Peanut Butter is by far my favorite, followed closely by Mocha. I found they mixed easily in both a blender and a conventional shaker bottle. Whenever I’m trying to cut weight, I find this delicious protein powder helps curb my sweet tooth and tide me over between meals.

While I didn’t personally experience this, some customer reviews mention it can be challenging to get in contact with Transparent Labs’ customer service team.

Jacked Factory Authentic Iso has 25 grams of protein per serving, 2 grams of carbohydrates, and just 0.5 grams of fat, which is the least amount of fat of any powder on our list. If you’re looking to lose weight, this macronutrient profile will help keep you on the right track. However, something to keep in mind: This protein powder is sweetened with sucralose, which is an artificial sweetener—studies link these sweeteners to increased cancer risk. Additionally, unlike most brands on our list, Jacked Factory doesn’t do third-party testing on its products. This means there isn’t a guarantee the ingredients are pure and match the ingredient label.

Kessler tried Jacked Factory Authentic Iso and was impressed. “This is the only protein powder I’ve tried that didn’t settle at all,” he says. “I found it a bit too sweet, but if you’re looking for a powder that tastes like dessert, you should opt for this one.”

If you’re looking for one of the best vegan protein powders that also works with a weight loss diet, Ka’Chava is a great choice. This vegan protein powder is marketed as a “whole-body meal,” which means it’s designed as a meal replacement rather than an addition to a meal or snack, like the other protein powders on our list. That’s why the calorie, carbohydrate, and fat counts (240, 25 grams, and 7 grams, respectively), are higher. The carb count is high for those on a low-carb diet, so that’s something to look out for. However, it packs in 25 grams of plant protein, derived from a combination of peas, brown rice, and quinoa, which will help preserve muscle while on a weight loss diet.

Tester Zoe Ettinger, a C.N.C.-in-training, uses this protein powder often. “I’m a big fan of Ka’Chava. It tastes delicious mixed in a smoothie with some frozen blueberries,” she says. “I also like that it also has adaptogens, probiotics, greens, and probiotics. I notice a difference in how good I feel when I take Ka’Chava regularly,” she says.

One thing to note about Ka’Chava is that it is the most expensive option on our list at $79.99 for a 15-serving bag. While the price reflects the fact that this protein powder is intended as a meal replacement, it’s still a big investment.

I chose Nutricost as the best protein powder for weight loss available on Amazon because its calorie and macronutrient profile is ideal for shedding pounds. Nutricost has a high protein content per serving, which is important for weight loss as protein can help enhance satiety and preserve muscle mass while in a deficit. With minimal fat and carbohydrates, this protein ensures you get the maximum protein intake without the added calories, making it an ideal choice for those looking to lose weight efficiently.

The taste and mixability of this protein are also top-notch. I tested the Vanilla flavor; it blended excellently in both milk and water and had an authentic vanilla taste profile. Despite using artificial sweeteners, which often make products sickly sweet, I found the sweetness level to be on point. However, if you’re trying to avoid artificial sweeteners, choose Promix or Transparent Labs, which use natural sweeteners.

Huel is our favorite meal replacement for weight loss because it has a great protein-to-carb ratio. Huel has 40 grams of protein per serving, the most of any protein powder on our list, and 24 grams of carbs. While this might be more carbs than ideal for those on a keto diet, it’s a solid portion for most. Carbs are an essential nutrient and according to experts, you can consume 100 to 150 grams a day and still lose weight.

Kessler tried Huel in Chocolate and Vanilla. “The Chocolate flavor was great, probably because it uses real cocoa powder, which gave it an authentic chocolate flavor,” he says. “The Vanilla wasn’t as good—it didn’t really taste like vanilla and had an artificial aftertaste.” He notes that it doesn’t mix very well, but says it made him feel great. “Other similar products, like Transparent Labs Mass Gainer, give me an upset stomach. But I felt great after taking Huel Black Edition,” he says.

Promix is our favorite clean protein powder because it’s third-party tested and results are easily viewable on Promix’s website. Those results show this product is tested for heavy metals and verified gluten-free. And beyond these positive results, this protein powder has one of the most simple formulas on our list. Vanilla, for example, has just four ingredients, and Promix doesn’t use any artificial ingredients.

This protein powder, like others on our list, has a solid protein-to-carb ratio for weight loss (25 grams to 7 grams, respectively). A 2020 study found consuming a higher portion of protein versus carbs helped participants lose weight and prevented them from gaining the weight back.

I tried the Vanilla flavor of this protein powder. I enjoyed it for the most part, but it wasn’t quite sweet enough for my taste. And I wish it mixed a little better—there were some clumps after mixing.

One thing to note about Promix is that while it has been third-party tested, it hasn’t been third-party tested for sport specifically. This means it hasn’t been tested for substances banned in athletic competitions. So if you’re an athlete planning to compete, opt for a powder that’s Informed Sport Certified or NSF Certified for Sport.

One of my favorite casein protein powders is Casein+ from Legion Athletics. I chose Casein+ because it’s all-natural, meaning it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors, and it’s third-party tested by Labdoor for purity and potency. This product provides 25 grams of protein per serving and only contains 110 calories, regardless of the flavor you choose. This protein-to-calorie ratio is ideal for weight loss.

Along with whey, casein is a type of protein found in milk and is characterized by its slow digestion and absorption. This prolonged digestion makes it an ideal option for people looking to manage hunger levels and maintain a consistent supply of amino acids over an extended timeframe—such as during sleep or when going a long time between meals. By providing a steady stream of protein to the muscles, casein helps mitigate the risk of muscle breakdown that often accompanies calorie restriction. As a result, incorporating a casein protein powder into your diet can be a strategic move to help support your weight loss goals.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., tried the Dutch Chocolate flavor, saying it reminded him of a dark chocolate bar that isn’t too rich or too sweet. The only downside is that casein protein has a different consistency than whey. It’s generally thicker and often takes longer to dissolve. Lunsford noticed this during his testing, saying the product had a “slightly chalky aftertaste.”

Naked Whey’s Unflavored protein stands out for its simplicity and purity; its single-ingredient formula consists of whey protein concentrate sourced for grass-fed cows. This simplicity aligns with the brand’s commitment to transparency, priding itself on avoiding additives, fillers, or artificial ingredients in its products.

With its neutral taste profile, this protein powder is very versatile, letting you integrate the protein powder seamlessly into your favorite recipes or smoothies without altering the flavor profile. Kessler tried the Unflavored version and says it “has a very slight vanilla taste to it.” He also detected a note of earthiness, but says “It would be really good mixed into a smoothie.” However, he mentions the two-scoop serving size can feel like a lot, so he recommends using extra liquid when blending it.

If you’re someone who prefers a flavored protein powder, you’ll be happy to know Naked also offers five flavored options, including Chocolate, Vanilla, Strawberry, Chocolate Peanut Butter, and Double Chocolate. Naked only uses coconut sugar to sweeten its protein supplements, which isn’t nearly as sweet as artificial sweeteners like sucralose or acesulfame potassium.

We chose Sports Research as our best protein powder for weight loss and muscle gain because it has a solid protein-to-calorie ratio (25 grams to 140 calories), is Informed Sport Certified, is fairly priced at $1.20 per serving, and tastes great, according to testers.

From a nutritional standpoint, Sports Research stacks up well against many of its competitors. The per-serving content for protein (25 grams), calories (140), and carbs (2 grams) compares favorably with most of the choices on our list, although the fat per serving (3.5 grams for Vanilla and 4 grams for Dutch Chocolate) is on the high side. Other ingredients include vitamin D, which has been linked to muscle health in recent research.

Tester Cory Kessler, C.N.C., C.P.T., tried the Creamy Vanilla flavor. “When I mixed it with milk it almost tasted like vanilla ice cream,” he says. “But when I mixed it with water it diluted the flavor, and all I could taste was the sweetness,” he warns. He also notes that it mixed very well, and “wasn’t gritty or clumpy at all.”

Whether from powder or whole food sources, protein aids weight loss mainly by:

Protein powder can be an effective tool in helping you achieve your weight loss goals. Drinking a protein powder shake or smoothie provides a quick, easy way to consume high amounts of protein with a limited amount of calories, fat, and carbohydrates. One of the main benefits of protein powder is that it’s often extremely lean, with a very high ratio of protein to total number of calories. This makes protein powder an efficient way to hit your daily protein target while adhering to your calorie guidelines.

Choose a protein powder with a significant amount of protein, typically around 25 grams per serving. If you have weight loss goals, a whey, soy, or pea protein isolate is likely your best bet since they are ultra-filtered to remove excess carbohydrates and fats.

When you have weight loss goals, it’s best to choose a protein powder with a moderate calorie count per serving, e.g., 100 to 160 calories. You should also ensure the majority of those calories come from protein, as this will best support your weight loss progress. Remember, protein is four calories per gram, so you can expect a supplement that has 25 grams of protein to have around 110 to 120 calories if it’s extremely lean.

It’s important to check the ingredients list of the supplement to ensure the product is free from added sugars or unnecessary fillers. Although these ingredients may contribute to the flavor, sweetness, and creaminess of the supplement, they often come with added calories. It’s generally best to select protein powders with minimal ingredients.

Occasionally, protein powders contain ingredients such as creatine, probiotics, or branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs). While these aren’t necessary, it’s important to assess whether these added ingredients align with your health and fitness goals, and whether it’s worth choosing a protein powder that offers these options.

Regardless of your goals, choose a protein powder with a flavor and consistency you enjoy. I know this seems obvious, but if you dislike the taste, then you’re far less likely to use the protein powder on a consistent basis, if at all.

As a certified nutrition coach, I advise my clients to choose a protein powder that’s been third-party tested for quality, purity, and safety, especially when I’m working with athletes. This ensures your supplement is free from contaminants, including banned substances, and is deemed safe for consumption. Third-party testing also holds supplement companies accountable, providing assurance that the ingredients in the product align with the information provided on the supplement facts label.

Whenever you’re purchasing a dietary supplement, you should look for one that aligns with your specific health and fitness goals. With weight loss in mind, it’s typically recommended to avoid products with added sugars, or excessive amounts of carbohydrates and fats. Some consumers may also choose to avoid products with artificial additives, such as sweeteners, flavors, and colors, which are routinely found in protein powder supplements. If you’re looking for an all-natural protein powder with minimal ingredients, consider Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey or protein powders from Naked Nutrition.

As a certified nutrition coach, I think it’s important to emphasize that a protein powder isn’t a necessity for weight loss success. However, due to its convenience and effectiveness, it does offer some notable benefits when used as part of a holistic approach to weight loss that includes resistance training, quality sleep, and healthy lifestyle habits. Consuming a high-protein diet, especially during a weight-loss phase, helps manage hunger levels and improves muscle preservation. If a protein powder can help you hit your daily protein targets while still maintaining a calorie deficit, then I think it’s worth incorporating into your regular routine.

Protein shakes are an excellent way to help preserve lean muscle mass when pursuing your weight loss goals. If weight loss is your primary objective, I’d suggest opting for a whey protein isolate, such as Transparent Labs 100% Grass-Fed Whey. This protein powder is incredibly lean, meaning the majority of calories come from protein alone. This can help you achieve your daily protein targets without over-consuming calories from the additional carbohydrates and fats commonly found in a whey protein concentrate.

Weight loss strategies vary from person to person, however, individuals with weight loss goals should aim for at least 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight. (This equates to approximately 0.5 to 0.7 grams of protein per pound of body weight.) This range should provide enough protein to support muscle mass while maintaining a calorie deficit, which is necessary for weight loss.

With protein powder for weight loss, certain protein sources are considered “leaner” than others. For example, whey protein isolates benefit from various kinds of processing and filtration that lower the fat and carbohydrates in the finished product. The main drawback with some plant-based proteins is that they can be naturally higher in carbs. Fortunately, high-quality plant protein powders could deliver comparable results to whey protein in terms of promoting lean body mass.Lean animal proteins include chicken breast, fish, and eggs. Even certain cuts of beef (sirloin) and pork (loin) are considered lean. Greek yogurt, tofu, beans, and lentils are among the non-animal sources of lean protein.

When focusing on weight loss, it’s best to steer clear of calorie-rich beverages such as sugary sodas and sports drinks, fruit juices, and alcohol. Instead, choose options like water, seltzer, black coffee, and unsweetened tea, all of which are essentially calorie-free. Avoiding calorie-dense beverages allows you to allocate those calories to food instead, which should help improve your satiety or feelings of fullness after meals.

There’s no protein that targets belly fat loss specifically. However, prioritizing lean protein, such as a whey protein isolate, can be beneficial for your overall weight loss goals. Whey protein isolates are processed to minimize the carbohydrate and fat content, maximizing the protein-to-calorie ratio of the supplement. This makes them an efficient option to support your intake of dietary protein while maintaining a calorie deficit.

There were many reasons to be excited about the 2026 Olympia Weekend in Las Vegas, NV, but one that got a lot of attention was the new Fit Model Olympia category. This inaugural show meant that every athlete who graced the stage was a part of bodybuilding history.

One of those competitors was Svetlana Fedkina, and she feels that fate and hard work were what led her to that moment.

“I remember when (IFBB Pro League Vice President) Tyler Manion announced the new Fit Model division in December 2024. My first thought was, ‘This is my chance. Maybe this is my path to the Olympia.’ Of course, I didn’t know that I would actually make it there, but for the first time in a long time, I saw a division where I felt I could truly show who I am as an athlete.”

Fedkina said that competing in bodybuilding shows felt like a natural continuation of her sports life, which included ballet for most of her childhood. She discovered the Bikini division in 2013 and could see herself competing in those shows.

“That’s really why I fell in love with bodybuilding. For me, it brings together everything I love: sports, discipline, constant self-improvement, aesthetics, and the opportunity to perform and express myself on stage.”

Fedkina enjoys competing but also acknowledges a higher purpose: inspiring people to improve themselves and make changes for the better.

She said, “I want people, especially women, to see that being strong and healthy can also be feminine and beautiful. If my own journey can inspire someone to become a better version of themselves, that means a lot to me.”

When the Fit Model category was announced, Fedkina saw an opportunity to train and showcase her ultimate form as an athlete. When she first started competing in Bikini, Ashley Kaltwasser was the reigning Olympia champion. Her look from back then was acknowledged by the IFBB Pro League as the inspiration and standard for this new division.

Call it inspiration or divine intervention, but Fedkina felt this was more than a new category for her to enter. The years of pursuing a pro card in her previous class may have seemed like failure at the moment, but now she feels they were stepping stones to this point.

“I also had this strong feeling that everything I had been through in the sport was somehow preparing me for this opportunity.”

She earned that coveted pro card in May 2026 at the Junior USA event. She made her pro debut one month later at the St. Pete Pro, taking eighth place. Then came Tampa. In only her second pro show, Fedkina not only took first place but earned an Olympia qualification as a result. That qualification culminated in a sixth-place finish at the inaugural Fit Model Olympia.

“Being part of the first-ever Fit Model Olympia was incredibly special to me,” she said. “It was a historic moment not only for our division, but for the sport of professional bodybuilding as Fit Model made its debut on the Olympia stage. I’m very proud that my name will always be part of that history.”

Regardless of the result, Fedkina already made her own history by becoming the first Slavic athlete to qualify for the Fit Model Olympia. While she is proud of that, she also understands it came thanks in part to timing and opportunity. She’s thinking more about what she can do with that accolade going forward, including inspiring other athletes to follow suit and join her on the Olympia stage.

“I hope it can inspire other women from that part of the world as well. Sometimes your opportunity doesn’t come when you expect it to. You just have to keep going long enough to be ready when it finally does.”

After starting 2026 as an amateur, she made her Olympia debut and left as one of the top six in her category, making her a potential contender to watch in 2027. As is the case with many world-class athletes, Fedkina has already set her sights on what is ahead and plans on finishing better than sixth if she makes it back onto the Olympia stage.

“That result gave me two things at the same time: confirmation that we did a lot right, and even more motivation because I can clearly see that there is still room to grow. It showed me that I can compete at this level, and it made me even more excited to see how far I can take this.”

Fedkina shared a lower body workout that she used during her Olympia prep. She feels that even though the standards are different from Wellness or Bikini, you still need to prepare for hard work when you go into the gym. She emphasized her setup of the Bulgarian split squats if this is a harder area for a lifter to develop.

“It is basically the only exercise I do all week that significantly involves my quads. Over time, I’ve developed a specific setup and technique, including using a resistance band around my working knee, that helps me shift most of the work toward my glutes.”

Fedkina typically rests for 1.5-2 minutes but will take as much as five for more difficult sets.

Replays of the 2026 Olympia can be seen at olympiaproductions.com. You can follow Fedkina on Instagram @sweetlana_ifbbpro.

#8686. My Shimano Pedals Are Nearly 10 Years Old—This 10-Minute Service Saved Me From Spending $200 on a New Set

A quick SPD-SL pedal service can revive old Shimano pedals—and help you avoid a costly update.

My longest-lasting pedals are a roughly 10-year-old pair of Shimano SPD XT pedals that have admittedly seen zero maintenance. Those pedals have been effectively abused on everything from getting bashed through rock gardens to long dusty or muddy days on the gravel bike. A few years ago I got my first road bike and switched to a pair of Shimano SPD-SL pedals. Since then I’ve put that bike (and those pedals) through the wringer.

I tend to stress test gear, even prior to having this job, so I enjoy taking my road bike out on everything from light gravel to singletrack that I have no business on. This means my road pedals have seen similar abuse to my mountain bike and gravel pedals. They’re still in great shape, but they could use a little love. Even pedals only used for road riding will start to get gritty over time.

Then I saw Shimano’s pedal release—not only are the old cleats not compatible with the new pedals, but the price of the new Shimano pedals starts at $200 for the Ultegra model and go up to $300 for the Dura-Ace model.

After I saw the rollout, it felt like a good time to bring my old generation SPD-SL pedals back to life and while I’m at it, give you a few tips on the process. Here we’ll run through how to service your SPD-SL pedals in under 10 minutes and save you a few hundred dollars in the process.

A quick note on reinstalling the pedals back on the bike: make sure you put the right pedal on the right side and the left pedal on the left side. I know, this sounds obvious. I’ve seen the wrong pedal get forced into the wrong side of the crank too many times, damaging the crank and the pedals to the point that sometimes both need to be replaced. Sometimes pedals are marked with an “L” for left and “R” for right, but you can always double-check to see which way the threads go. Left pedal threads will go up to the left and right pedal threads go up to the right. Then when it is time to reattach the pedals, put some grease on the threads of the crank arm and begin to thread them on by hand instead of starting with the wrench. If you can’t begin to thread the pedal onto the crank threads by hand, double-check the pedal is on the correct side, make sure it’s going into the crank arm straight, and make sure there is no debris in the hole of the crank arm preventing it from threading.

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:

Most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

For a married couple receiving substantial Social Security benefits, that could represent tens of thousands of dollars of annual income that they don't have to generate by selling investments.

On Episode 308 of The Menace Podcast, host Dennis James was joined by Milos Sarcev and Chris Cormier, and the trio discussed Michal Krizanek’s big bodybuilding win in Slovakia. With momentum on his side, should Krizo now enter the 2026 Arnold? Apparently not, they suggested.

Slovakian mass monster, Michal “Krizo” Krizanek crushed his competition in Kosice on October 25 and took first place in the IFBB 365 Grand Prix Pro, but what’s next for the big man as he prepares to pump his career up a level in 2027?

#8683. The 5 Best Outdoor Saunas for Getting Your Sweat On in 2025

Experts explain how hot and cold wellness therapies could improve health. These outdoor saunas help you get these potential benefits at home.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.

There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves. Some newer models have high-tech features like surround-sound speakers, added LED light therapy, and charging docks for your electronics. However, all you need to reap the potential benefits of your sauna experience is a high-quality product you’ll actually use.

We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you. We also tapped Saloni Sharma, M.D., Medhat Mikhael, M.D., and Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher studying exercise science and Sport and Health Sciences faculty member at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland (a.k.a., sauna central), to help us understand how sauna use can benefit athletes during training.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re seeking a more technology-forward sauna experience, Sun Home’s Luminar outdoor infrared sauna is an excellent model to invest in. This five-person model uses an infrared heating system, which you can control through your phone via a mobile app. Indoor saunas often have infrared heat, but Sun Home claims its Luminar model is more than 12.5 times more powerful at 500 watts than competitors. This sauna includes Bluetooth speakers and soothing LED chromotherapy, making sitting in a hot room more enticing to beginner bathers. Yes, it’s a pricey model, but it has ample features and floor-to-ceiling windows for a panoramic view of the outdoors.

According to SweatTent, you can set up the SweatTent Outdoor Sauna in about three minutes. It is somewhat portable because it is simple to put up and take down. The material is durable, insulated, and weather-proof, so you can leave the sauna outdoors indefinitely.

A wood-fired stove heats the SweatTent and comes with 20 pounds of sauna rocks, a fire poker, and heat-resistant gloves to feed the fire safely. The SweatTent is our favorite option for a complete sauna kit. It’s easy to set up, comparatively inexpensive, portable, and works well.

The Sun Home Luminar Sauna is a cube sauna with a carbonized wood exterior and dura-glass windows built to withstand any climate conditions. Luminar has a compact footprint compared to other two-person cube saunas. It uses a combination of infrared and full-spectrum heaters positioned to maintain optimum heat regardless of exterior conditions.

The choice of grade-A carbonized red cedar wood and thick double-pane glass throughout the sauna ensures durability and insulation. With nine heaters, including three far-infrared heaters under the bench and six full-spectrum heaters surrounding the cabin, the Luminar Outdoor Sauna guarantees an efficient and effective sauna session. Sun Home places these heaters strategically to envelop the users in 3D healing wavelengths from all angles.

You can control the Luminar temperature from an app to start heating your sauna before you get home. It has Bluetooth surround-sound speakers and a panoramic view through the dura-glass windows.

The Redwood Outdoors Barrel Sauna is a traditional barrel sauna made with Thermowood. It has all the features you need with nothing extra. We appreciate that you can customize several parts of this dry sauna, from the heating mechanism (you can go the Finnish sauna route with a Harvia electric heater or a wood-burning stove) to add-ons like a weather-resistant shingled roof and even a cold plunge tub. It has a spa-like sauna scent and dry heat, and comfortably fits four to six people.

One benefit of a Thermowood sauna is its durability and resistance to the elements. Redwood Outdoors says that, when properly cared for, this sauna should have an outdoor lifespan of 20 years.

The Redwood Outdoors Thermowood Cabin Sauna is our best outdoor sauna for cold climates because of its robust, weather-resistant construction. This sauna has a traditional Scandinavian design with Scandinavian softwood treated with intense heat to provide exceptional insulation. This design enhances its longevity and contributes to its energy efficiency, ensuring even heat distribution throughout the interior.

The Thermowood Cabin Sauna package includes a Harvia electric heater, wooden heater guard, water bucket and ladle, sauna rocks, and interior seating benches, providing all the necessary components for an authentic sauna experience.

If you’ve spent quality time in the locker room sauna, you’re committed to the wellness practice, and you live somewhere with outdoor space, a sauna might be an excellent investment for your health. “Researchers have found several possible health benefits from sauna use; most importantly, they have shown to help cardiovascular diseases—particularly high blood pressure and heart diseases—as well as acute and chronic pain and neurological diseases,” Mikhael says.

Putting a sauna inside can create some logistical challenges, though, from installation to insulation and more. An outdoor sauna might be easier to install, and it gets you closer to nature, as many of them have spacious windows. “One big bonus of outdoor saunas specifically is they exist outdoors,” Sharma says. “There is a problem in our society labeled Nature Deficit Disorder, which means we aren’t spending enough time outside. There are many proven benefits of being outdoors, and these saunas allow you to combine them with the potential benefits of heat therapy.”

Depending on your model, once your outdoor sauna is installed and ready to go, you can set the temperature via a manual dial, Bluetooth-enabled app, or touchscreen. The heat comes from sauna heaters or wood-burning stoves. Some outdoor saunas allow you to set the timer up to 36 hours in advance. From there, all you need to do is open the door, climb in, and relax.

As for timing, “Two to three 15- to 25-minute sessions per week are ideal,” says Mikhael. “After 15 to 25 minutes, people can benefit the most without feeling like they’re getting dehydrated or dizzy.”

Bring a book, crank up your music, or bring a friend to sweat it out with you—and remember to stay hydrated.

“You want to ensure you’re hydrated before and after,” says Sharma. “A sauna induces a lot of sweating, so you can get dehydrated very easily.” We recommend an electrolyte powder after use if you sweat a lot.

Ideally, you should be heading to your sauna soon as part of your post-workout routine, Lee says. “We found not only is a combination of exercise and sauna bathing stronger in its effects, but many cardiovascular benefits, like lower blood pressure, were sustained for a longer period afterward.”

Most saunas use electricity to run the lights and heaters. Low-tech wood stove-heated saunas might not need any power if there are no lights. There are some solar-powered saunas, too, if you want less strain on the environment (and your electric bill). You’ll just need to make sure you have a battery as a backup.

Given their size and weight, saunas are not very portable. So we’d recommend buying an outdoor sauna once you’re living in a permanent residence rather than an apartment or rental. But even then, life happens, and sometimes you need to move. You can move a constructed outdoor sauna, but it would likely need professional equipment to hoist it into a truck bed. There are very portable tent saunas—much more affordable than the outdoor ones on our list.

The outdoor saunas we recommend cost between $1,599 and $9,799. Based on our research, the lower end of the spectrum offers plenty of heat but fewer bells and whistles. The more pricey saunas can typically seat more people, have more temperature adjustments, provide more comfortable accommodations, and are made with higher-quality materials.

Many outdoor saunas on this list offer additional accessories a la carte. While these aren’t integral to your new sauna routine, they might make it more fun, luxe, and/or comfortable. Some standard accessories we noticed are outdoor showers, cold plunge tubs such as the Plunge, and wooden recliners. Nothing’s stopping you from DIY-ing those accessories, though.

Many wellness fads are short-lived trends (and even potentially harmful). But saunas have been staples in Scandinavian life for centuries, showing significant promise in improving your well-being. Our experts say regular sauna use can improve muscle soreness and even chronic pain.

If you’ve dabbled in heat therapy in the past and want to make it more of a long-term lifestyle (and you have the budget to match), an outdoor sauna can be a valuable and beneficial tool. But, like any significant investment in your health, our experts say you should always consult your doctor before purchasing an outdoor sauna or starting a sauna routine—especially if you have severe cardiovascular or lung issues.

The cost of an outdoor sauna depends on several factors, including capacity, heat source, extra features, integrated technology, and materials. We found saunas at around $1,599 and others at up to $9,799, depending on your budget and needs.

Yes, outdoor saunas typically come with features and accessories to help weatherproof them (like shingles) and keep them dry and ventilated during winter.

When investing in an outdoor sauna, you have to consider its costs, including the electricity used by electric heaters, lighting, and more. When purchasing an outdoor sauna, look for the wattage and amount of electricity it needs to run; it doesn’t hurt to crunch the numbers to estimate your electric bill with a sauna in the mix.

#8682. I Dug Through Garmin’s Black Friday Deals—These Are the Bike Computers, Cycling Radars, and Smartwatches Worth Your Money

Save on editor-picked Garmin bike computers, Varia radars, smartwatches, trainers, and power pedals.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Electronic devices always make great holiday gifts for cyclists. Whether you’re buying for a rider in your life or upgrading your cycling computer, radar, smart trainer, or power meter on a budget, Black Friday is the best time to score big savings. And Garmin makes some of the best and most popular training and navigation devices for road, gravel, fitness, and mountain bike riders.

Garmin’s GPS computers, smartwatches, radar taillights, power pedals, and Tacx indoor trainers have received great reviews from Bicycling editors and top rankings in our head-to-head tests. The brand’s gear doesn’t often go on deep sale, so these early drops are worth jumping on before they sell out. However, with so many models marked down across both categories, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed. Plus, devices can look similar at first glance, but the details matter when choosing the right tool for riding, training, and everyday fitness.

SHOP GARMIN DEALS ON AMAZON SHOP DEALS ON GARMIN.COM

Garmin GPS head units are one of the smartest upgrades you can make to your road, gravel, mountain, or electric bike, and a much safer alternative than strapping your phone to the bars to see your route. Cycling computers also capture, process, and display data from accessories like heart rate monitors, power meters, and even electronic shifting to help you ride better, train smarter, and stay connected. And because Garmin lets you customize nearly everything—from data fields to navigation screens—you can tailor exactly what shows up.

Buying Tip: Buying previous-generation cycling computers is a great way to save money. Older models usually have almost the same performance at a big discount. Cyclists often even prefer the old models if they’re lighterweight or have better battery life.

Cycling radar is one of the most important pieces of bicycle technology released in the last decade. On-bike radar systems mount to the rear of your bike and feature an integrated taillight. Paired with a cycling computer or smartwatch, they notify you about vehicles approaching from behind so you can move out of the way. They are a must-have item for road and gravel riders.

Buying Tip: Garmin is a pioneer in cycling radar tech and makes the most reliable, consistent systems. The Varia RTL515 is our benchmark and best-value pick, while the RearVue 820 is newer and more powerful; it’s our choice for best performance. The RCT715 is the 515 with an integrated rear-facing camera.

While dedicated cycling computers are the go-to choice for road, gravel, and data-heavy training, many riders prefer Garmin’s smartwatches because they keep everything in one place, especially when they track more than bike rides—anyone who mixes riding with running, hiking, paddling, strength training, or even walking the dog. Garmin watches have powerful GPS, workout metrics, and daily health data in a streamlined device that’s always with you (and they even tell time).

Buying Tip: Mountain bikers often appreciate the simplicity and safety of recording their rides from the wrist rather than risking a pricey head unit in a crash. Triathletes, duathletes, and cyclocross racers love the seamless transitions a watch allows. There’s no need to swap devices or merge files after an event.

Most riders know Garmin from its computers, smartwatches, and cycling radar. But Garmin also owns the indoor trainer brand Tacx. Its smart trainers and indoor bikes are highly regarded for their excellent performance, integration, and useful features. One cool feature we love—especially if you live somewhere prone to winter power outages—is that the Neo 2T generates its own resistance electromagnetically. That means you don’t have to scrap your workout plans just because the lights go out.

Buying Tip: Smart trainers are great for riding in virtual worlds like Zwift. For a deep dive into more great indoor trainers and buying info, check out my story “Ready to Ride Indoors? Here’s How to Pick the Best Trainer.”

Garmin Tacx Neo 2T with Zwift Cog and Click

Want to step up your training for next season? The best way to measure cycling gains is by training with power—and for that, you need a power meter. Power pedals, like Garmin’s Rally series, are easier to install than crank-based power meter options. Plus, you can swap power pedals easily between bikes. This not only saves cost, but it also gives you consistent data from bike to bike.

Buying Tip: Garmin offers a handy option to buy its power meter in a package including two pedal styles (road and mountain bike/gravel) with swappable spindles. This way you can measure power across riding disciplines.

Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. #8681. Wilde Wins Second Race of Weekend as Taylor-Brown Takes Down Derron at T100 Dubai

Less than 24 hours after his third-place finish at WTCS Abu Dhabi, Hayden Wilde (NZL) showed few outward signs of fatigue as he hit the front of the race in T1, rode among the leaders, and ran his way to victory ahead of training partner Kyle Smith (NZL).

Georgia Taylor-Brown said before the race that she wanted to “beat Julie,” and her wish came true. A small breakaway in the swim put Derron (SUI) on the back foot from the start, while Taylor-Brown had to overcome cramps on the bike and a charging Nicole Van Der Kaay (NZL) on the run to earn a narrow, yet important victory.

It was a mixed cast of T100 veterans and rookies on the men’s start line, with several notable names absent after the men’s Saudi Arabia T100 race was moved to Dubai on short notice.

Big news leading into the race was that RaceRanger devices would not be used on the bike due to customs delays in getting the equipment into Dubai, leaving officials to enforce the 20-meter draft zone without the light sensor system.

A large group emerged from the tepid water to start the bike. After a subpar swim left Wilde chasing in Abu Dhabi the day before, he not only swam with the front group but sprinted through transition, smiling and chatting as he rounded Rico Bogen (GER), showing little sign of the previous day’s effort.

He took his time putting on full-length aero socks as Menno Koolhaas (NED) went straight to the front to lead the men onto the scorching tarmac for 80km of time trialing on the flat course.

The group of 17 after the swim quickly whittled down to 10 as average speeds approached 30 mph in the opening stages.

As Bogen, Wilde, and Smith continued to push the pace, the group quickly dropped to just six. The standout name among the group was Mika Noodt (GER), back racing for the first time since his collision with an ambulance at Ironman 70.3 Swansea in July and already taking turns at the front.

Noodt had been one of the sport’s biggest up-and-coming stars before the accident and was to be Wilde’s strongest challenger on the T100 circuit this year. He has openly shared the mental struggles and trauma that followed the crash, but it seemed he was back to full strength on course as the German powered toward the run.

Off the bike, a quick transition saw Wilde round Bogen for the lead, and he looked set to run away without a challenge. Smith, however, quickly moved alongside him and stayed there for the opening laps until Wilde turned up the heat.

From there, there was no stopping him as he put last year’s lap-counting drama in Dubai behind him to head into the Qatar final with a perfect score from his three counting results. Smith held on for his best T100 result of the year, ahead of an emotional Noodt, who marked his return with an immediate trip to the podium.

One of the most remarkable revelations came afterward, when Wilde shared that he believed he had raced much of the day with a broken toe. He injured it during the Aussie exit on the swim and, thinking it might be dislocated, tried to pop it back into place during the bike. Despite the swelling afterward, he said it had not troubled him too much on the run.

A front group of four broke away early on the swim as Taylor-Brown and Kate Waugh’s (GBR) plan to put Derron under pressure from the start worked perfectly. Waugh led through the Aussie exit before Sara Pérez Sala (ESP) led the group into T1.

Derron found herself almost a minute down, but alongside strong riders Caroline Pohle (GER) and Van der Kaay, she remained well within contention. The big question was whether her efforts in Kona would affect her race or whether the heat preparation would prove beneficial in the sweltering conditions.

On the bike, it appeared to be the former as Pohle and Van der Kaay left her behind and worked their way to the front. They eventually helped put more time into Derron, who was over two minutes back and still losing ground on the third lap.

It was not an unfamiliar position for Derron, who had overcome a deficit at the previous women’s race in Vancouver to take down Taylor-Brown and Waugh.

However, it soon became clear that only Taylor-Brown would remain in the fight for the win, with Waugh’s race unraveling in the heat. She later shared on social media that she had started the race sick but still managed to get across the line in ninth, her first T100 finish off the podium.

Everything was going according to plan for Taylor-Brown until she began suffering from adductor cramps late on the bike. She lost positions as she tried to soft-pedal them out, but thankfully for her, they subsided enough for her to start the run just 36 seconds behind Pohle, with Van der Kaay and Pérez Sala also ahead.

Taylor-Brown’s cramps were well in her rearview as she quickly made up the gap and began building a lead. By the third lap, it looked as though that advantage might continue to grow all the way to the finish.

However, Van der Kaay was putting together the best T100 performance of her career and began closing again heading into the final lap. Derron had moved into third but was not making any significant inroads into either athlete ahead.

Van der Kaay put in one final surge to try to catch Taylor-Brown but came up just 10 seconds short. The victory now sends Taylor-Brown into the Grand Final six points clear of Derron and in pole position to become world champion.

Van der Kaay’s excellent performance, which included the second-fastest bike and third-fastest run, moves her into third in the standings heading into the final.

#8680. Canyon’s PACE Cockpit Has a Clever Answer to One of Integrated Bars’ Biggest Problems

Five drop shapes and three width settings add flexibility to a proprietary cockpit.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Integrated cockpits can be light, aerodynamic, and good-looking. They can also make simple jobs harder than they need to be. Adjusting your position can mean cutting a steerer tube. Replacing a broken handlebar can mean buying a whole new cockpit. And routing brake hoses through everything can turn a small change into a long afternoon.

I’ve given Canyon’s PACE system plenty of criticism in my reviews. It’s proprietary, and integrated systems come with real compromises. But after swapping the drops on the Endurace CF SLX 9 I have in for review, I want to give Canyon credit for a thoughtful design choice.

The main section of the PACE cockpit is called the T-Bar. Canyon’s system lets you adjust cockpit height by up to 20 mm in 5mm increments, without cutting the steerer. The cockpit is also made up of three pieces, with the drop sections bolted to the T-Bar. That offers a couple of advantages.

First, it makes the bar width adjustable. The T-Bar has three width positions, 25 mm apart, for a total range of 50 mm. The actual widths depend on the drop shape. See the table below.

The bolt-on drops also let Canyon offer five shapes with different dimensions. If the drops that come on your new Canyon don’t suit you, you can swap them for another option.

My Endurace review bike came with the Compact drops. They have a 108mm drop, width settings from 390 to 440 mm, and 8 degrees of flare. I prefer a narrower bar with a deeper drop and more flare, so I switched to Canyon’s Control drops. They have a 120mm drop, adjust from 370 to 420 mm, and feature 17 degrees of flare.

*U.S. prices at the time of writing. Bar tape and fixing screws are included.

Here’s what I needed to do to make the swap: unwrap the bar, loosen and slide off the controls, remove the old drops, install the new ones, then tighten everything and rewrap the bar. Canyon includes fresh bar tape with the replacement drops.

Canyon also includes a clever cardboard tool that helps you evenly align your controls. I loved it!

With most one-piece integrated cockpits, switching to a different bar shape or replacing a broken drop means replacing the whole assembly. Depending on the bike’s routing, that may also mean disconnecting or replacing brake hoses and bleeding the brakes.

On the PACE, the brake hoses run behind the drop sections rather than through them, so I didn’t have to disconnect or cut them. That meant no brake bleed, no risk of ending up with a hose that’s too short, and no replacing the entire cockpit.

That also matters if you crash and break a drop. With a one-piece handlebar and stem, a broken bar can mean replacing the whole assembly. With PACE, you can replace the damaged section.*

*If you break a drop, check the PACE T-Bar, or stem, for damage, too. Replace it if necessary.

The system can also make bike travel less nerve-racking. If your bar tape is set up so the controls can slide on and off without rewrapping, you can unbolt the drops and let them hang out of the way. The bike packs a little narrower, and the handlebar ends are less exposed to side impacts. I’ve had bars damaged in transit more times than I can count, so I appreciate this feature.

PACE is still proprietary, and those concerns don’t disappear because one part of the system is clever. But integrated cockpits often force riders to accept limited adjustability, few shape options, and costly replacements. Canyon has found a useful way to make its handlebar easier to fit, repair, and travel with. For that, it deserves some credit.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#8679. The Best Power Racks of 2025: Our Top Picks for Strength Training

Our expert shares his experience, and an Olympic lifting titleholder shares advice on choosing the best option so you get stronger with this home gym staple.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

A power rack allows you to safely perform weightlifting exercises like barbell squats and bench presses, without a spotter, in your home gym. Add-on accessories like pull-up bars, dip stations, and resistance bands can help you get the most out of your power rack, giving you the tools for a versatile full-body workout.

Whether you have limited space or are looking for a budget-friendly power rack, there are options that may work for you. We compiled a list of the best power racks for your home gym with all the details you need to find the right equipment to take your fitness routine to the next level in 2024. Shane Sevcik—a USAW-1 (USA Weightlifting) certified coach, current USA Weightlifting Foundation board member, state record holder, and Masters Pan American and World title holder—also shares his insights into what to look for in power racks.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

The REP Fitness PR-1000 Power Rack has a four-post frame made from 14-gauge steel with laser-cut holes spaced two inches apart. There are two pull-up bars—one is 1.25 inches thick, and the other is two inches thick—so you can do accessory work such as pull-ups and grip exercises without using additional space or buying a separate piece of equipment. The pull-up bars are strategically placed on the rack, spanning the front and back posts, contributing to the overall stability. There are built-in weight storage pegs on the back base for additional sturdiness. You can customize the rack using multiple accessory options such as safety straps, a dip station, and more.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., CF-L1, used this rack to do exercises like squats, bench press, strict press, pull-ups, and more for almost two years. He describes it as an intermediate or beginner rack and noticed movement while un-racking 350 pounds. “The rack held the weight just fine, but there was some swaying after I removed the bar. I’d recommend it to a beginner or someone who doesn’t lift to that capacity because I was happy with it otherwise.”

We like that the PR-1000 comes with chrome-coated safeties extending past the rack, offering an additional place for a barbell. The numbered uprights allow you to adjust the safeties or J-hooks quickly and never have to worry about your bar being crooked. “The J-hooks were easy to move, and the hole spacing of one inch is adequate to get the bar lined up where you need it,” Lunsford says. “I can attest to the functionality of the safeties; they worked great for me when I failed a heavy bench over 250 pounds.”

The Titan Fitness T-3 Series Power Rack is a wall-mounted power rack that folds to a closed position, which only sticks out five inches from the wall. The bolt-down uprights and side bracings keep it stable, so you feel comfortable lifting weights to 1,100 pounds. Those who want to use the dual pull-up bars for dynamic movements such as kipping pull-ups or toes-to-bar benefit from the added stability the floor attachment provides. The rear pull-up bar is two inches thick, and the front pull-up bar is the industry standard of 1.25 inches thick.

This rack is made from 11-gauge steel and features two-inch by three-inch tubing. Typically, newer racks have three-inch by three-inch steel tubing, so attachments from other brands may not work. Lunsford says, “A rack is an essential piece of fitness equipment. What sets them apart is the build, value, and accessories. A full power rack of this style with a weight capacity of 1,100 pounds for around $400 is an excellent bang for the buck.”

Lunsford says the brand uses manufacturing processes to elevate the overall quality. “The holes are laser cut instead of punched, and the brand uses robot welders instead of guides operated by humans.” This technique allows for more efficiency, precision, and consistency in enhanced craftsmanship. The laser-cut holes are two inches apart, and the bench and clean pull zone have Westside hole spacing—holes in the upright that are closer together for more precise positioning.

Free shipping is available on all Titan products, and a one-year warranty covers manufacturing defects and issues that may arise while using the product. One callout we have is the rack does not come with safety arms, which range in price from $90 to $190, depending on which type you get. The rackable weight capacity is 1,100 pounds, but the included J-cups are rated up to 1,000 pounds, so if you want to move heavier weights, you’ll need to upgrade the J-cups.

Titan offers several accessories for purchase separately, including safety bars or straps, stabilizer feet, spotter arms, pin and pipe safety set, or an extension kit to upgrade to six uprights. Other customization options include choosing from a black, red, or blue rack color, two rack depths and heights, or adding a four-pack of weight plate holders.

At only 72 inches tall (six feet), the REP PR-1050 Short Power Rack is a solution for home gyms with low ceilings, such as garages or basements. This equipment has a sturdy yet compact footprint of 58 by 48 inches and supports up to 700 pounds.

While this power rack is short, it provides a solid range of features. It comes with dual pull-up bars (supporting up to 400 pounds), numbered upright holes spaced two inches apart, rear base weight horns, chrome-coated safeties, and plastic-lined J-cups. It’s also compatible with various add-on attachments, including cannonball grips for grip strength exercises and landmine attachments for exercises including landmine presses and rows.

The Fringe Sport Retractable Power Rack is an excellent option if your garage or home gym is tight on space because it is compact and easily stored. This convenient home power rack can be retracted and folded inward or outward for storage. When retracted, it only sticks out five inches from the wall. It has a compact base and can support up to 800 pounds.

The uprights are two-by-three-inch 11-gauge steel and feature Westside spacing in the bench zone. You can set the rack’s 1.25-inch diameter pull-up bar to multiple heights. It’s 91 inches tall, which may not be ideal for low ceilings.

The unit comes with J-hooks coated with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMW), a strong, abrasion-resistant material, to protect your barbell. Fringe Sport provides an installation video to help guide you through the installation of this power rack. It includes four mounting brackets and six detent pins to lock the rack in position.

The Sunny Health & Fitness Power Zone Strength Rack Power Cage Squat Rack has a pulley system attachment for lat pulldowns and adjustable resistance you can load with weight plates up to the 352-pound limit. You can use the lat pulldown attachment for exercises like upright rows and curls. When you aren’t using the attachment, built-in safety hook latches provide easy storage for the top long or short lever bar.

This power rack has features to help you get a well-rounded workout. The adjustable angled pull-up bar has four positions, including wide and narrow grips. The J-hooks have 18 vertical height settings, and the spotter bars with safety latches help you squat with heavier weights. There are six resistance band pins, for additional resistance against the bar.

The Rogue Fitness R-3 Power Rack is the most compact option in Rogue’s R-Series and is an excellent option for a home garage gym. This power rack comes in two height options—90.4 inches or 84.4 inches—so it works in garages and home gyms with low ceilings.

This rack is made of heavy-duty 11-gauge steel with Westside spacing (a type of spacing that allows for granular control of bar placement, such as barbells and safety bars) through the bench in a one-inch pattern and two-inch spacing above and below the bench. The unit is compatible with various Rogue Infinity Series add-on attachments, such as the Rogue Matador, fully adjustable dip handles, or a bar hanger for barbell weight storage.

The unit has a 43-inch pull-up bar, infinity J-cups, pin/pipe safeties, and four band pegs. You can customize this rack by adding a bar, bench, or plates to your purchase on the Rogue Fitness website. This unit is versatile enough for various exercises, including low rows, pull-ups, chin-ups, squats, bench presses, powerlifting, CrossFit, and Olympic lifting.

The Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has an official weight capacity of 800 pounds. This unit can help anyone hit their goals, from beginners to elite powerlifters.

Like all good squat racks, the Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has solid steel safety arms rather than hollow tubes. It features two rear stability bars. Thanks to 19 adjustable height levels, you can use the unit for various exercises besides squats, including pull-ups, chin-ups, bench presses, and overhead presses. And it’s $299, the most affordable option on our list.

It has a multi-grip pull-up bar and two 23-inch safety bars with chrome locks. While it doesn’t come with J-hooks, dip bars, or plate storage attachments, one-inch holes allow you to use this equipment with standard-sized attachments.

A power rack—or power cage—has four uprights designed to serve as a base for powerlifting, Olympic lifting, and other strength training. They are commonly used with a barbell but may have optional attachments for non-barbell exercises using cables or body weight. A full power rack allows athletes to lift inside or outside the cage. Half racks have two uprights, so athletes must lift outside the rack because there is less depth.

Research links strength training, including weightlifting, to long-term health benefits like reducing disease.

A power rack provides equipment, like safety bars, to help you lift heavy weights safely without a spotter. Some power racks come with add-on attachments, such as pull-up bars and dip bars, to help you get a well-rounded workout. Additionally, most power racks are compatible with accessories you can buy for an extra price to customize your workout for your needs.

Exercisers use a power rack for strength training, Olympic lifting, and powerlifting. Additional attachments, such as a dip station or pull-up bar, allow you to use it for bodyweight exercises. Some have pulley systems for other resistance exercises.

Correctly using a power rack can successfully enhance strength training. “It’s all about consistency,” Sevcik says. “Make sure you have some kind of progressive overload built into your programming.”

Power racks provide a safe lifting experience, which is of utmost importance, especially if you plan on training alone. The safety straps, pins, or arms—also called safeties—are a critical safety feature. “One of my biggest pet peeves is when I see people who don’t know how to set the safety arms the right way and have the pins set way too low,” Sevcik says. “The purpose of those safety arms is to give you a safe way to bail out of a lift. Otherwise, you’re just using a power rack as a big immobile squat stand.”

So, what is the correct way to set up the safety arms? “To set them up for squats, put the unloaded bar on your back and squat down to the deepest position you can get yourself into,” Sevcik says. “The safety bars should be about an inch and a half or one notch lower than your bottom position, so if you ever fail on a squat, all you do is sit your butt down to the very bottom.”

Many come with safety arms, pins, or nylon straps, but some budget options may require purchasing them separately. If you’re new to using a power rack, we recommend asking a fitness professional for guidance on different exercises and safety.

Before purchasing, measure your space and look at the rack’s total footprint. While measuring the floor and comparing it to the base is essential, ceiling height is another crucial factor. You may need a shorter option if you use your rack in a basement or a room with low ceilings.

You can retract and store a folding power rack if you’re limited in space or need room for other activities. It’s a good idea to consider your height and weight when looking at the dimensions, especially if you plan to use the pull-up bar or other attachments. You may want to leave space on each side for accessories so you can attach them on the sides if necessary. We recommend you keep the space around the rack clear of obstructions, particularly in front, so you can safely complete your lifts or bailout.

Power racks come in a variety of styles, colors, and materials. Some construction and style factors to consider include:

The power racks on this list have capacities ranging from 700 pounds to 1,100 pounds. The lower and middle weight range will likely work for you if you are a beginner or intermediate exerciser. If you are an advanced athlete, you may want to opt for a power rack with a high weight capacity and heavy-duty steel. Attachments such as safety arms, J-hooks, or pull-up bars have varying weight limits. Always stay within the recommended weight range for your safety.

How much you’re willing to spend depends on your budget and training style. Many racks on this list include a basic setup, with the option to add accessories as needed, which cuts the cost. Other racks come fully loaded with accessories, so they are incredibly versatile. However, these options cost more, so it is crucial to consider the features and whether or not they are helpful for your workout style and goals. The racks on this list range from around $299 to $965, and many brands offer free shipping.

Power racks come in various styles and features. The following sections break down Sevcik’s power rack must-haves.

Sevcik says to look for thick, heavy-duty steel such as 11-gauge. “A rack made out of thicker steel creates more leverage on the uprights. Especially when you add those attachments.”

“I think a big must-have a lot of people overlook is to make sure your J-cups, or J-hooks, have some coating on them to preserve the knurling on your bar,” Sevcik says. “If you’re doing a bench press or deadlift, [knurling] is no big deal, but if you’re an Olympic weightlifter, that’s where my snatch grip is holding onto, and I want it to be as sharp and aggressive as possible.”

“I would make sure you have enough hole patterns to make a lot of adjustments. Sometimes, they’re too spaced out, for example, in two-inch increments instead of one,” Sevcik says. “I like to have the added adjustability, especially for those heavier weights.”

Sevcik says having the option to do pull-ups is a good idea. “They’re one of the most basic, fundamental movements. Plus, if you dedicate the square footage to put the rack in there, you’ll want to get as much utility as possible because you are sacrificing some real estate.”

“It’s important to have the option to add accessories,” Sevcik says. “You might not want a dip bar right now, but down the road, you may decide to incorporate more dips in the training program, and it sure is nice to have your power rack as your one central piece of equipment.”

Many power racks come with attachments, though certain brands require you to purchase add-on attachments separately. Some of the power racks on this list come with pull-up bars (chin-up bar), safeties, and J-cups included, while others do not. It’s important to read the details of what comes with your unit to know what additional purchases you’ll need to make to achieve your desired power rack workout.

We considered the following while choosing each product on this list:

We chose budget-friendly and high-end options suitable for any fitness level and listed several compact and folding options for those with limited space. We also spoke to Shane Sevcik, a USAW-certified coach and competitive athlete, about essential add-ons and safety features.

Research suggests 30 to 60 minutes a week of muscle-strengthening exercises can benefit your health. With the help of a power rack, you can achieve a wide range of strength training fitness moves without needing a spotter. A power rack can add convenience to your workout by enabling you to get a safe weightlifting workout anytime from the comfort of your home gym.

A full power rack has four to six uprights attached by cross members, creating a cage to lift in. A squat rack—also called a squat stand—is typically two uprights and weighs less than a power rack, making it more portable. Power racks are more versatile, with the option to add accessories, while squat racks usually do not.

If you choose a freestanding power rack, anchor it following the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure it’s safe and secure.

Generally, a freestanding power rack should be a few feet from the wall so you can perform exercises comfortably and safely. Always refer to the manufacturer’s guidelines and recommendations when setting up your rack.

Common gauges are 11-gauge and 12-gauge, with lower numbers providing thicker and stronger steel; however, these tend to be more pricey options. A thinner 14-gauge steel is slightly less sturdy but likely works well for a general home gym setup. We chose racks ranging from 11-gauge to 16-gauge to suit various budgets and fitness levels.

Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC, is a writer and editor in the fitness and nutrition industries. She has contributed to PowerliftingTechnique, FeastGood, Garage Gym Reviews, BarBend, and Fitbod. When she's not working, you can find her training in her garage gym; cuddling with her dog, Charlie; trying to keep her two cats, Raven and Riley, from destroying her house; or hanging out with her family - all with a cup of coffee close by.

#8678. How Yonatan Katz Cracked the Boulder Nobody Could Solve at the World Climbing Series

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Climbing is what happens when you take a gym rat’s obsession with grip strength, remove the floor, and let gravity do its thing. There’s no bench to lie on, no belt to tighten, and no place to hide a weak link. You have to get your body up a wall using holds that sometimes look so bleak the edge of a credit card looks like it might offer more purchase. And if you screw up, you better hope your rope is knotted correctly.

That was on full display at the World Climbing Series bouldering finale in Salt Lake City, October 16-18. In the men’s final, Israel’s Yonatan Katz won gold on only his second start in the senior international series. He went into the final problem behind Britain’s Maximillian Milne and came out the winner after pulling off a move nobody else in the final had managed.

Here’s how it happened. The last boulder was a nasty coordination problem. Before Katz stepped up, the other finalists who had attempted it hadn’t even reached the scoring zone, a designated hold partway up the route. On his fourth try, Katz got past the zone and reached the top. He finished with 69.7 points. Milne couldn’t answer on his turn and took silver with 59.7. Japan’s Rei Kawamata was third with 54.2. For a sport that looks, to outsiders, like a bunch of people climbing a wall, there was a hell of a lot of drama hanging off those holds.

The women’s final the next day had its own story. France’s Oriane Bertone won with 84.6 points after being the only finalist to complete the first boulder. Britain’s Erin McNeice finished second with 69.7, barely ahead of Japan’s Mao Nakamura at 69.6. McNeice didn’t win that night, but she won the season-long Boulder title. She’d opened the series in 11th place and followed it with a gold and four silvers.

Meanwhile, Japan’s Sorato Anraku had already locked up the men’s overall championship after winning five of the six bouldering events. Then he failed to advance from qualification in Salt Lake City. Even the guy who dominated the season can get humbled by a fresh set of plastic holds. If bodybuilding judges replaced their comparison rounds with problems that changed every week, we’d see a few interesting faces backstage.

Bouldering is done on relatively short walls with thick mats instead of ropes. The athlete has to solve a sequence of moves, reach designated holds, and control the top. Strength matters, obviously. So does the ability to position your hips, push through your feet, generate momentum, and decide what to do before your forearms turn into concrete. Some moves are slow and surgical. Others look like a gymnast being thrown into a hardware store. The best climbers aren’t simply pulling themselves upward. They’re figuring out how to make the least-wasteful movement possible under pressure.

There’s a lesson in there for anybody who trains. A giant back and a crushing handshake don’t automatically make you good at something that requires timing, balance, and technical skill. Nor does being smaller make you weak. Climbing exposes the difference between owning strength and knowing how to use it. And if you’re tempted to try it, start with an introductory session, not an advanced overhang and a heroic declaration. A 2026 review of 45 climbing-injury studies found frequent problems involving fingers, hands, shoulders, and ankles. Those little finger pulleys weren’t designed to absorb your entire ego on day one.

I like sports that punish bullshit. Climbing is high on that list. There’s no score for looking intimidating while you chalk your hands, and no bonus for explaining how strong you’d be if the holds were bigger. Katz won because he solved a problem that had stopped the others. McNeice took the season because she kept delivering. The wall doesn’t care about your résumé, your physique, or your excuses. It only cares whether you can get to the top.
